_sources: AVSAB position statements, ASPCA, AKC, Fear Free, Cornell Riney Canine Health Center, Merck Veterinary Manual, VCA, UC Davis. Research: Ziv 2017; Vieira de Castro 2020; Herron 2009; Horowitz 2009; Hart 2018; Sueda & Hart 2008; Pauli 2006.

rules.b: No shouting, no scruffing, no muzzle-holding, no alpha rolls, no spray bottle, no leash jerk, no shutting her in a room. This is the position of the American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior: there is no evidence aversive methods work better, and there is evidence they cause harm. Herron 2009 measured what happens when people try them: growling at the dog provoked aggression in 41 percent, forcing something from her mouth 39 percent, an alpha roll 31 percent.

rules.t: She cannot connect a telling-off to something she did minutes ago.
rules.b: Horowitz 2009 tested this properly. The guilty look tracks being scolded, not the misdeed; the most guilty-looking dogs were innocent ones told off anyway. Scolding her over a puddle teaches her that eliminating in front of a person is dangerous, so she learns to go behind the sofa. Your accident count drops while the problem gets worse.

rules.t: At ten weeks almost everything here is a management problem, not a training problem.
rules.b: If you are helping out, your job is prevention and de-escalation. You are not running behavior programmes on someone else's puppy.

rules.t: Two things that matter more than any technique.
rules.b: Enzymatic cleaner for every accident, never ammonia based, because ammonia smells like urine to her and re-marks the spot. And a harness, never the collar, for anything with leash tension. Pauli 2006 measured a significant rise in eye pressure when force went through a collar but not a harness. Her collar carries the ID tag and nothing else.

entries.title: She needs 18 to 20 hours of sleep a day
now: Eighteen to twenty hours a day at this age. Most of it. That is not a puppy being lazy, that is what her brain needs to build.
Roughly an hour up, two hours asleep. If she has been awake more than about an hour and she is getting wild, that is the clock, not her character.
Put her in the crate for a nap BEFORE she falls apart, not after. A puppy who is already over the edge cannot settle on her own.
Sleep is when learning consolidates. A short training session followed by a nap does more than a long session does.
not: Do not try to train, correct or reason with an overtired puppy. She cannot take food and she cannot think. Crate, dark, quiet.
Do not assume more exercise will tire her out. Past a point it winds her up further. Sniffing and chewing tire a puppy far more reliably than running does.
entries.why: This is the single most useful thing a new owner can know, and almost nobody is told it. The frantic biting in the evening, the zoomies, the suddenly deaf puppy who knew her name an hour ago: that is overtiredness, and it looks exactly like naughtiness. If you take one thing from this section, take this one. Half the problems in this guide are the same problem.
entries.vet: A puppy who is hard to rouse, or sleeping far more than usual AND flat when awake, is a different thing. Same-day call.

entries.title: The four times she always needs to go out
now: AFTER SHE WAKES UP. Every time, from any nap, not just the morning. This is the biggest one and the most missed.
AFTER SHE EATS. Her own log says one to two hours, which is slower than most puppies, so learn her timing rather than the textbook.
AFTER SHE PLAYS. Movement moves things along.
AFTER ANYTHING EXCITING. A visitor, a delivery, a game, coming out of the crate.
Plus, at this age, roughly every hour or two anyway.
The rule that covers all of it: if something just changed, take her out.
not: Do not wait for her to tell you. A ten week old does not yet know she needs to go until she is already going. Asking her to signal you is a skill she does not have for weeks yet.
entries.why: House training is not really about teaching her to hold it. It is about arranging for her to be outside at the moments she was going to go anyway, and then paying her for it. Get those four right and the accidents mostly stop on their own.

entries.title: The house leash: how to actually stop accidents happening
now: Six foot leash. One end on her harness, the other clipped to your belt or belt loop. She goes where you go.
She can still play, still have toys, still lie down. You are just always holding the other end.
The point is not restraint. It is that you are present at the two seconds before it happens, when she starts sniffing the floor or circling, and you can get her out.
When you cannot be attached to her, shower, cooking, going out: crate or pen. That is what they are for.
Loosen it in stages once she has had about a week clean: leash off but same room, then same floor, then free run.
If accidents come back, go back a stage. That is information about your pace, not about her.
not: NEVER tie her to furniture and walk away. She can tangle it and choke. The leash goes on YOU, and only while you are actually there.
Do not give her the run of the apartment when you are not sure she emptied outside. If you did not see a proper squat, treat her as full.
entries.why: You cannot interrupt what you cannot see. Every accident that happens out of sight is a rep that trains the floor, and the relief is its own reward, so it gets paid whether you are watching or not. The house leash removes the opportunity entirely rather than trying to correct after the fact, which does not work anyway because she cannot connect it. Most people need a few weeks of this. It feels like a lot on day one and then it stops being noticeable.

entries.title: What is actually normal at ten weeks, so you stop worrying about it
now: Biting and mouthing constantly. Normal, developmental, not aggression. It softens over weeks if you are consistent.
Hiccups, often after eating or excitement. Normal and they pass.
Sleeping in odd positions, twitching and paddling while asleep. Normal.
Crying in the crate the first several nights. Normal, and it gets better if the crate work is done properly.
Zoomies, usually evening. Normal, and usually a sign she is overtired.
Eating grass occasionally, in a puppy who is otherwise well and passing normal stools. Usually not sinister.
Not finishing every meal, some days. Normal, as long as she is bright and her weight is climbing.
Three to five poops a day. Sleeping most of the day. Wanting to chew everything.
not: Do not compare her to an adult dog, or to a puppy you saw online. Ten weeks is very young.
Do not read a single odd day as a trend. Look at the week.
entries.why: First-time owners spend a lot of energy worrying about things that are simply what puppies do, and then sometimes miss the things that matter because everything feels alarming. The point of this entry is to give you back that energy for the things in the vet section.
entries.vet: What is NOT normal and is worth a call: lethargy that persists, refusing food for more than one meal, repeated vomiting, blood in stool, pale gums, straining, or a puppy who is simply not herself. When in doubt with a ten week old, call. They go downhill faster than adult dogs.

entries.title: The deadline nobody tells you about
now: Her socialisation window runs from about 3 weeks to about 16 weeks. She is 10 weeks now. What she learns to accept before it closes, she accepts for life.

Aim for new experiences every day, in small calm doses: different people, hats, beards, umbrellas, wheelchairs, children at a distance, traffic noise, lifts, stairs, tiled floors, hoovers, hairdryers, doorbells.
CARRY HER for the risky surfaces. A sling or your arms. She can see and hear a whole city without her feet touching ground that unvaccinated dogs have toileted on.
Handling counts and is easy to forget: ears, paws, mouth, tail, being held still, being lifted. Every one of those pays for itself at every vet visit for twelve years.
Quality beats quantity. One calm good experience is worth more than five overwhelming ones.
not: Do not force her into anything she is frightened of. Pushing a scared puppy through it does lasting harm rather than getting her used to it. Let her retreat, go further away, and try smaller.
Do not wait until her vaccines are finished. The window closes at roughly the same time the vaccine series completes, and there is no second chance at it.
entries.why: There is a genuine tension here and anyone who pretends otherwise is oversimplifying: she is not fully vaccinated, and parvo is real. But more dogs under three years old are put to sleep for behaviour problems than die of infectious disease. The answer is not to choose one, it is to socialise deliberately while choosing safe surfaces. Carried, in your building, in friends homes with healthy vaccinated dogs, on clean hard surfaces. Not dog parks, not pet shop floors, not grass where unknown dogs toilet.
entries.vet: Ask your vet where they draw the line locally. They know what is circulating in your area, which you do not.

entries.title: If you are exhausted and wondering what you have done
now: This is extremely common and it has a name. People call it the puppy blues. Almost nobody admits to it and most first-time owners feel some version of it.
It is worst somewhere in the first two to six weeks, and it lifts.
Practical things that genuinely help: use the crate for HER naps so you get your hands back, accept help when it is offered, and let some things be imperfect for a few weeks.
Get out of the apartment without her sometimes. She has to learn to be alone anyway, so a short absence is training, not neglect.
Sleep matters for you too. Broken nights are what makes everything else feel unmanageable, and they do end.
not: Do not take it as evidence that you have made a mistake, or that you are bad at this. Feeling flattened by a ten week old is not a verdict on you.
Do not measure yourself against how it looks online.
entries.why: It belongs in a guide because the surprise of it is half the problem. People expect to feel delighted, feel wrung out instead, and then feel guilty about that on top. Naming it takes most of the weight off.
entries.vet: If it is not lifting, or it is affecting your sleep, appetite or mood more broadly, that is worth talking to your own doctor about. That is a real thing and it is not about the dog.

entries.title: Progress is not a straight line, and regression is normal
now: Expect good weeks and bad weeks. A puppy who was clean for four days and then has three accidents has not forgotten anything.
Look at the week, not the day. Your log is for exactly this: compare this week to last week rather than today to yesterday.
When something gets worse, the useful question is what changed. New food, a new person, a growth spurt, a disrupted routine, teething, less sleep.
If a skill falls apart, drop back one step and rebuild. That is not starting over, and it usually takes days rather than weeks.
not: Do not respond to a bad week by adding pressure. Almost always the answer is more management and less asking of her.
Do not conclude the training does not work after three days.
entries.why: Learning in dogs is not linear and neither is physical development. A five month old who has apparently forgotten everything is a normal five month old, not a failure of training.
entries.vet: A sudden clear regression in house training, in a puppy who was reliably clean, is worth ruling out medically before you treat it as behaviour.

entries.title: What is coming: adolescence, and why to do the work now
now: Roughly five to eighteen months. She will get bigger, bolder, and noticeably worse at listening. This is normal and it is temporary.
The classic signs: recall falls apart, she starts noticing other dogs far more, and she tests things she had accepted for months.
The work you do at ten weeks is what you will be leaning on then. Recall, leave it, settle, handling, and being alone are all far cheaper to build now.
Keep training through it in short sessions. Keep her on a long line outdoors during the worst of the recall wobble rather than losing the behaviour entirely.
Teething runs from about 12 to 16 weeks and finishes around six or seven months. Chewing gets worse before it gets better and she needs legal things to chew.
not: Do not assume a dog who is ignoring you at eight months has forgotten. She has not. She is choosing, and the answer is to make yourself worth choosing, not to punish.
entries.why: Most dogs given up to shelters are adolescents, not puppies. Knowing it is coming, that it is normal, and that it passes, is most of what gets people through it.
entries.vet: Neutering timing is a real conversation for a golden retriever specifically, and it belongs in this window. See the guide entry on it and ask your vet directly.

entries.title: Set this up tonight, not at 2am
now: Look up your nearest 24 hour emergency animal hospital NOW and put the address and number in all three phones. Do it before you need it.
ASPCA Animal Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Twenty four hours, there is a fee.
Pet Poison Helpline: (855) 764-7661.
Your own vet, and their out of hours arrangement, which is often different from their main number.
Know her weight and keep it updated. Every emergency call starts with it.
Keep her microchip number and her vaccine record somewhere you can reach from your phone.
A photo of her food bag, including the ingredient panel and the lot code, on your phone.
not: Do not plan to look this up at the moment you need it. At 2am with a frightened puppy is the worst possible time to be searching.
entries.why: Nearly every genuine emergency in this guide is made better by five minutes of preparation done on a calm evening. The point is that a person who is not you might be holding her when it happens.
entries.vet: Worth asking your vet at the next visit: who do you use out of hours, and where should I take her.

entries.title: What to actually buy, and what to skip
now: A crate with a divider, sized for her adult weight, so you only buy one.
A Y shaped harness and a six foot leash. Two leashes if you can, one for the house.
A five metre long line for recall work outdoors. Not a retractable.
A Kong Puppy, the softer blue or pink rubber, not the red Classic.
A lickmat with suction cups. Cheap and it does a lot of work at bath time and in the crate.
A snuffle mat or any food puzzle. Sniffing tires her more reliably than walking.
Enzymatic cleaner, a big bottle, and buy it before you need it.
Heavy non-tip stainless or ceramic bowls. One for food, and one for water in every room she uses.
A slicker brush and a comb.
Soft training treats you can break into quarters.
not: Skip the retractable leash. It teaches constant tension, which is the opposite of what you want.
Skip choke chains, prong collars and anything that works by being unpleasant. There is no version of her life where those are needed.
Skip antlers, hooves, rawhide and hard nylon. See the chews entry.
Skip most soft toys for unsupervised time. Stuffing is a swallowing risk.
Do not buy a bed you cannot wash. Get one with a removable cover.
You do not need most of what a pet shop will sell you. The list above is genuinely most of it.
entries.why: The expensive mistakes are the crate you outgrow and the equipment that makes training harder. Everything else can wait.

entries.title: Reading her poop: what the 1 to 7 score actually means
now: THE TEST: pick it up. Does it leave anything behind? That one question separates most of the scale.
1 — separate hard little balls, like rabbit droppings. They roll. Picks up leaving nothing. TOO HARD.
2 — log shaped but lumpy, clearly made of pellets stuck together, and it often breaks into pieces. Firm, picks up clean. STILL TOO HARD.
3 — a smooth log. Firm, holds its shape, picks up clean and leaves nothing on the ground. THIS IS THE ONE YOU WANT.
4 — log shaped but soft. Loses its shape when you pick it up and leaves a mark behind. A bit loose.
5 — piles rather than logs. Very moist, no real shape, hard to pick up cleanly.
6 — mushy, no shape at all.
7 — liquid. A puddle.
Short version: 3 picks up clean and holds together. 1 and 2 are too hard. 4 and up are too soft.
If you did not look properly, tap Skip. A guessed number in the record is worse than a gap.
not: Do not score from memory hours later. Look at the time, or skip it.
Do not read one odd stool as a problem. It is the run of them that matters.
entries.why: The scale exists so that three people can describe the same thing the same way, and so that a week of stools can be compared rather than remembered. It is only worth anything if everyone scores it the same, which is why the pick-up test is the wording here rather than words like firm or ideal, which mean nothing until you already know the answer.
entries.vet: Two days running at 5 or above is a vet question, not a training one. So is several days running at 1 or 2, especially in a puppy passing only one or two stools a day when three to five would be normal. Take the actual scores and times, not a description.

entries.title: She had an accident on the floor
now: Caught in the act: one small neutral sound, an uh-oh or a light clap. Just enough to pause her, not to frighten her. Then carry her to the toilet spot.
If she finishes in the right place, pay her there and then. Praise plus two or three treats, at the spot, not once you are back inside.
Found it afterwards: clean it, say nothing, note the time. That is the whole protocol.
Enzymatic cleaner. If it smells like a toilet to her it stays a toilet.
not: No scolding, no pointing at it, no nose-rubbing, no shutting her in a room.
Do not startle her hard mid-pee. Sources differ on whether to interrupt at all; the safe version is the smallest sound that gets her to pause.
entries.why: An accident is a scheduling miss by a person. Out on waking, within fifteen minutes of every meal, after every play bout, and at least every two hours between. Look at the thirty minutes before it happened; almost every accident traces back to a missed trigger.

entries.title: How to tell whether she actually emptied outside
now: STOP LOOKING AT THE GROUND. Watch her body. She squats, so the squat is the evidence, not the puddle. On wet grass or after rain you will never see the puddle and you do not need to.
A real pee: she stops, maybe circles once, lowers into a squat and HOLDS STILL FOR 5 TO 15 SECONDS.
Not a real pee: a quick dip and back up in a second or two. That is a dribble, not an empty, and it fools everyone.
Actually count it. One, two, three. Under five seconds and she is not done.
Use pavement rather than grass. You can see it, you can hear it, and there is no dew to confuse you.
Same spot every single time. Her own smell prompts her, and you learn what her normal looks like.
WAIT FOR TWO. Puppies often go twice, a big one and a smaller one a few minutes later. Do not leave after the first.
Say a quiet word while she is actually going, not before. Go pee, every time, during. In a few weeks you can say it and she will go on request, and then you never have to wonder again.
not: Do not assume a squat means she is empty. A short squat and a full empty look similar and are not.
Do not bring her in and give her free run when you are not sure. If you did not see a proper squat, treat her as full: crate or leash for fifteen minutes and go straight back out.
Do not stand there for two minutes and give up. Emptying needs her to relax, and two minutes on a busy sidewalk is not long enough for a ten week old.
entries.why: This is the failure that makes everything else look broken. You think she went, so she comes in and gets freedom, and twenty minutes later there is a puddle on the floor. It is not that she prefers the floor in that moment, it is that she was never empty. On grass with dew on it there is no way to check afterwards, so the only reliable signal is what her body did at the time.
entries.vet: If she squats repeatedly and produces very little each time, that is not a training question. Frequent small volumes, or going again within minutes of being emptied, is worth ruling out medically.

entries.title: She rings the bell constantly
now: Count first. Write down every ring for two days: the time, and whether she actually eliminated. The answer is in that list and not in your memory of it.
If she goes most times she rings, she is not spamming it. She is a puppy with a small bladder telling you the truth. Keep going.

If she rings and does not go: take her out anyway, on the leash, straight to the spot, stand still and boring for two minutes, and bring her straight back in. No walk, no sniffing tour, no hello to anybody.
Make sure a bell trip is the ONLY thing that ever follows a ring. Walks and play start at a different time, or from a different door, and never immediately after.
Keep her scheduled trips running. A puppy taken out often enough has less to ask for.
not: Do not start ignoring rings. That is how you get an accident, and a dog who stops telling you anything at all.
Do not tell her off for ringing. She is doing exactly what you taught her.
Do not rip the bell down in week one out of frustration. If it really is useless, take it down deliberately and tell the other two, so nobody quietly puts it back.
Do not add a second bell, or a soundboard button, in the hope that one of them will be the clear one.
entries.why: The bell means 'the door opens' unless you make it mean 'I need to pee'. What decides which one she learns is entirely what happens on the other side of the door. If a ring sometimes produces a walk, a game or a neighbour, she will ring for those too, and she will be right to.
entries.vet: Ringing much more often than usual, small amounts, straining, or blood is not a training problem. See she keeps squatting.

entries.title: She will pee happily indoors but not outside
now: PAY IT THE INSTANT SHE FINISHES, OUTSIDE. Within two seconds, with food, while her feet are still on the pavement. Not praise when you get back in. She cannot connect a reward indoors to something she did outdoors two minutes ago.
Take good food out with you every single time. Chicken or cheese, not kibble. This is one of the two things worth spending real value on.

STOP ENDING THE WALK WHEN SHE GOES. If peeing outside is immediately followed by going home, she learns that holding it makes the walk last longer. After she goes, carry on for another five minutes of sniffing. That is the payment.
If she does NOT go outside, she does not get free run of the apartment when you come in. Crate or a lead attached to you for fifteen minutes, then straight back out and try again. Repeat.
If she DOES go outside, she gets thirty to forty minutes of freedom indoors. That is the deal, and it is the single most effective piece of management here.
Give her longer outside. A five minute trip where she spends four minutes sniffing may not leave her time to actually go. Stand still in one spot and be boring for a few minutes.
Clean every indoor accident with an enzymatic cleaner, properly soaked and left the full time. Any spot that still smells of urine to her is a spot she will use again.
not: Do not scold her, show her the mess, or rub her nose in it. She cannot connect it, and what she learns is not to go in front of you, which is far worse and much harder to undo.
Do not assume she is being stubborn or spiteful. She is not.
Do not stand outside with her for two minutes and then give up and go in. That is the pattern that teaches her indoors is where it happens.
entries.why: Two things are happening and both are learning, not defiance. FIRST, dogs form surface and place preferences. Every successful pee on your floor is a rep: the relief itself is the reward, so the floor gets reinforced every single time it happens, whether you are watching or not. If the count is running five indoors to three outdoors, the floor is winning on volume. SECOND, a city sidewalk is an overwhelming place for a ten week old who is not fully vaccinated. Traffic, other dogs, noise, a hundred smells. Emptying a bladder requires a degree of relaxation, and an overstimulated puppy often cannot do it, then goes the moment she is home and calm. That is not her preferring your floor for its own sake, it is her only being relaxed enough to go once she gets there. The third cause is the one people never spot: if going outside reliably ends the walk, she has a reason to hold on.
entries.vet: Peeing small amounts frequently, or going again shortly after being emptied, is worth ruling out medically before you treat it purely as training. In a young female golden it is a specific thing to ask about. She has done it several times in the log.

entries.title: What should go in the crate, and what should not
now: One flat washable layer to lie on. A crate pad, a folded towel, or her bed.
Something to rest her head against is fine, and for some puppies it genuinely helps them settle. Dogs like a raised edge to lean on. That is why bolster beds exist.
Check everything every morning. You are looking for tooth marks, a pulled seam, or a corner starting to come apart.
Divider set so she can stand up, turn around and lie down. No more than that.
Re-check the whole arrangement at 12 to 16 weeks. That is when the adult teeth push through and chewing steps up sharply. A puppy who ignored her bedding at 10 weeks may start shredding it at 14.
not: Do not keep soft bedding in there if she is soiling it. Absorbent bedding wicks urine away, so she is dry and comfortable a minute after peeing, and that removes the only thing motivating her to hold it. If she pees on it, strip the crate to the bare tray for a week, then put one layer back once she has had seven clean nights.
Do not keep anything she has started to chew. The moment you find a seam open or stuffing showing, it comes out that day. Swallowed fabric is a blockage, and a blockage is surgery.
Do not stack three soft layers. A pillow and a towel and a bed together give her somewhere to move away from a wet corner, which is exactly what the crate size rule exists to prevent.
entries.why: Two separate questions get muddled here, and they have different answers. CHEWING is about this individual puppy: if she does not touch her bedding, the risk is low right now, and you will see it change before it becomes dangerous as long as you check daily. SOILING is about the mechanism crate training runs on: most puppies will not lie in their own mess, and absorbent bedding removes that discomfort. So the honest rule is not a blanket no. It is: soft bedding is fine while she is neither chewing it nor peeing on it, and the day either of those changes, it comes out.
entries.vet: Repeated crate soiling in a puppy who was previously clean can be medical. Mention it.

entries.title: She is crying or barking in the crate at night
now: Crate stays beside the bed. Put your hand down so your fingers touch it. That alone settles many puppies.
Tell fussing from distress. Grumbling and shifting that resettles within a minute or two is fussing, leave it. Escalating, screaming, panting, scrabbling at the door is distress, respond.
If she has been asleep two hours or more and starts up, assume bladder. Carry her out so she does not fully wake, no talking, no play, no treats, straight back.
A frozen stuffed Kong at lights-out, and an unwashed t-shirt of Ariel's in the crate.
not: Do not let her scream herself out. It can build a lasting bad association with the crate, and if you lose the crate you lose the tool everything else depends on.
Do not lift her into your bed at 3am. Once is enough for her to learn that screaming produces the bed.
Do not open the door at the peak of a protest bark. Wait for one breath of quiet.
entries.why: Sources genuinely disagree on whether to ignore night crying and there is no controlled trial. Everyone agrees on the fussing versus distress line, so use that rather than a rule.

entries.title: She peed or pooped in her crate
now: Get her out and straight to the toilet spot, calmly. She may not be finished.
Everything out of the crate. Wipe her clean with a warm damp cloth and dry her properly with a towel. No bath at 9pm.
Enzymatic cleaner on the tray, left for the time the label says. Bedding in the wash, pre-treated, cool or warm, never hot: heat sets the stain and kills the enzymes.
Clean dry layer down before she goes back in.
not: Do not scold her, show her the mess, or rub her nose in it. She cannot connect it, and what she learns is to hide where she goes.
No ammonia based cleaner.
Do not read the guilty look as understanding. It is a response to your face and tone.
entries.why: Most puppies will not soil where they sleep, so a fouled crate usually means the crate is too big, she was left too long, or she was already holding it. Check the divider is set so she can stand, turn and lie down and no more. If it keeps happening, fix the schedule, not the puppy.
entries.vet: Repeated crate soiling can be medical. Mention it.

entries.title: Toys in the crate: which ones, and why most should come out
now: What can stay in overnight: a Kong or solid one-piece rubber toy. Nothing that can have a piece torn off it.
Everything else lives outside the crate and comes out when you are there to watch.
Check whatever stays in, every morning, for tooth damage.
not: No stuffed or plush toys. Same swallowing problem as a pillow.
No squeaky toys. She will get the squeaker out, and it is small, hard and exactly swallowable.

NO ROPE TOYS. This is the worst one and the one people assume is safe. Swallowed strands become a linear foreign body, which can saw through the intestinal wall. It is a serious surgical emergency and it is worse than a solid object.
Nothing with eyes, tags, ribbons or glued-on parts.
Do not fill the crate with interesting things. If it is full of stuff to do, it is a playpen. You want somewhere nothing happens and she falls asleep.
entries.why: The crate is specifically where she is unsupervised. Every toy in there has to be safe with nobody watching for eight hours, which is a much higher bar than a toy you hand her while you sit on the floor with her. A stuffed frozen Kong is the exception worth making: it is safe, it gives her something to settle with at bedtime, and it can be filled from her measured ration so it costs nothing against her treat budget.
entries.vet: Retching with nothing coming up, a swollen or painful belly, vomiting after drinking, or straining with no stool means a possible blockage. That is surgical and hours matter.

entries.title: She is scratching and digging at her bedding
now: Usually nothing. Circling, scratching and digging before lying down is normal nesting, the canine version of fluffing a pillow.
If she is shredding rather than arranging, take the bedding out and give her a chew instead. Swallowed stuffing is the real risk, not the digging.
If it happens every time she is confined and comes with panting and scrabbling at the door, that is not nesting. See the alone entry.
not: Do not tell her off for a normal pre-sleep ritual.
Do not leave her with shredded fabric she can swallow.

entries.title: She is waking too early
now: Say nothing. No eye contact. Get up on an alarm, not on her noise.
If she genuinely needs to pee, take her: dark, silent, boring, straight back to bed. No lights, no breakfast, no chat.
Feed breakfast twenty to thirty minutes after you are up, not the moment you are up.
Drape part of the crate and run a fan or white noise. Garbage trucks and hallway noise are real inputs here.
not: Do not start the day at whatever hour she picks. Unlike night crying, this one is not contested: early waking really does get reinforced.
Do not scold her at 5am. You are adding attention to a puppy who is now fully awake.
entries.why: Fix it over days: set your alarm five minutes earlier than her current wake time for a week, then push it five minutes later each week. She learns the alarm starts the day, not her barking.

entries.title: She has gone wild and bitey this evening
now: Stop. Stand up, fold your arms, disengage completely. End the interaction.
Quick toilet trip.
Crate or pen with a chew or a stuffed Kong, delivered calmly and cheerfully with a treat. This is a nap, not a punishment, and it must never be delivered angrily.
Leave her. She may complain for a few minutes and then crash hard. Expect that.
not: Do not read it as surplus energy and play harder or go out again. An overtired puppy looks exactly like an over-energised one. That is the whole trap.
No grabbing her muzzle, no scruffing, no pinning, no shouting.
entries.why: Say it out loud: the frantic bitiness is the sleep deprivation. That is why the answer is a nap and not a walk.

entries.title: The bed is soiled and there is no time to wash it
now: Best: any clean dry substitute. A folded bath towel, a blanket, a fleece, a clean sweatshirt. It does not have to be dog bedding, and it takes thirty seconds.
Second best: wipe the tray with enzymatic cleaner, let it dry, and give her the bare crate floor. A bare floor beats a soiled bed.
Wipe her down and dry her before she goes in. A damp puppy on damp bedding is the worst combination.
Set an alarm for a toilet trip in two to three hours.
not: Do not just flip it over. The scent and the damp are still there.
Do not spray perfume or air freshener over it.
Do not move her to your bed or the sofa as a workaround. One night of that teaches a fast learner something you will have to undo.
Do not skip drying her because she seems fine.
entries.why: Two reasons, neither about tidiness. Lying in urine is genuinely irritating to skin, and the smell tells her the crate is a legitimate toilet, which undoes the housetraining she is in the middle of.
entries.vet: If her skin looks red or raw where she has been lying, say so.

entries.title: She fell asleep and a potty trip is due. Wake her, or let her sleep?
now: Let her sleep. Almost always.

Take her out the SECOND she wakes. Not after you finish the sentence, not after you find your keys. Waking up is one of the four times a puppy reliably needs to go, along with after eating, after playing and after getting excited.
Have your shoes and her leash by the door before you sit down to anything. The 60 seconds you spend hunting for them is the 60 seconds the accident happens in.

Know what waking up looks like: shifting and repositioning, a stretch and a shake, a whine or small bark, standing up. Circling is not a warning, it is the last step before it happens. Circling means go now.
The one time you DO wake her: last call at bedtime. There the alternative is nine hours of holding, which is a different problem from a 45 minute nap.
not: Do not carry a sleeping puppy downstairs to try to make her go. She was not about to. You have just woken her and restarted the clock.
Do not treat a missed slot on the schedule as a failure. The schedule is a default for when nothing else is happening. A sleeping puppy overrides it.
entries.why: She needs 18 to 20 hours of sleep a day at this age, and sleep is when learning consolidates. Most of what looks like a badly behaved puppy is a tired one: the biting, the zoomies, the completely ignoring you. Waking her costs you more than an accident does. And dogs do not eliminate while asleep, so a sleeping puppy is not one who is about to go. The urge has gone quiet and it comes back when she wakes, which is exactly why the moment she wakes is the one that matters.
entries.vet: A puppy who is genuinely difficult to rouse, or who is sleeping far more than usual and is flat when awake, is a different thing entirely. That is a same-day call.

entries.title: She will not settle. Pacing, will not lie down
now: Toilet first, always. Pacing is the classic I-need-to-go tell.
Then shrink her world: pen or crate, lights down, no talking, no eye contact. A loose puppy in an open room cannot switch off.
Give her a licking or chewing job. Frozen stuffed Kong, lickmat, safe chew.
Sit nearby and be boring. When she lies down, keep being boring.
not: Do not read pacing as needing more exercise and play harder or go out again. That escalates it and you get a wilder puppy twenty minutes later.
Do not repeat settle, settle, lie down. Talking to her is attention, and attention is fuel.
entries.why: In the evening, pacing is nearly always toilet, over-arousal, or overtiredness. All three are answered by confinement plus a chew, not by more activity.

entries.title: She is biting my hands, sleeves and ankles
now: Freeze. Go still and let your hand go limp. Jerking away triggers the grab reflex and makes it a better game.
Put something legal in her mouth, a toy or a chew, and praise her for taking it. She is a retriever; she is supposed to want something in her mouth. Give her the right something.
If she escalates, get up and leave for ten to sixty seconds. Behind a baby gate or out of the room. Then come back and try again.
Third time in ten minutes means she needs a nap, not a training session. See the overtired entry.
not: No muzzle-holding, no scruff-shaking, no fingers down the throat, no smacking her nose. Hitting can make a puppy bite harder and can produce fear and aggression.
Do not jerk hands or feet away. It looks like prey.
Do not let her use hands as toys, not even once.
entries.why: The classic yelp-like-a-hurt-puppy is the most published technique and it excites some puppies into biting harder, especially high-arousal retrievers. Try one calm flat ouch, once. If she escalates, drop it and use freeze then redirect then leave.

entries.title: She is chewing the furniture, the rug or a cable
now: Cables are the emergency: unplug first, then deal with the puppy. Do not lunge at her while she has a live cord.
Neutral uh-oh, take the item, and immediately hand her an approved chew and praise her for taking it.
Then fix the room, which is the actual solution. Cables behind furniture or in cord covers, power strips off the floor, shoes in a closed cupboard, laundry in a hamper.
If you cannot supervise, she goes in the pen. A puppy loose in a room she can chew is a management failure.
not: Do not tell her off for chewing you find later. She cannot connect it.
Do not rely on bitter spray as the plan. Individual variation is enormous and some dogs acquire a taste for it. It supplements puppy-proofing, it does not replace it.
Do not crate her for long stretches as the answer to chewing.
entries.vet: If she has bitten into a live cable, or swallowed fabric or plastic, that is a vet call now.

entries.title: She has her paws on the counter or stole food from the table
now: Clear the surface. Right now. That is the intervention.
Redirect her away and reward her on the floor, away from the counter.
Baby-gate the kitchen while you cook and eat, or pen her.
Food into containers or cupboards, nothing on the edge, bin secured.
not: Do not rely on catching and correcting. This is a slot machine: one sandwich, once, keeps her checking for months. You cannot out-correct an intermittent jackpot, only remove it.
Do not feed her from the table or the counter, ever, including a crumb.

entries.title: She growled at me over food or a toy
now: Stop moving. Stand up. Back away. Give her space. The growl is doing its job. It is information, not an attack.
If it is her food or a legal chew, leave the room. Let her finish. Collect the bowl later.
If it is genuinely dangerous, a chicken bone or medication, do not grab and do not corner her. Scatter food away from her, or lure her into another room and shut the door.
Prevent the next one: feed her behind a closed door or in her crate, pick up high-value chews before people are around.
not: Never punish the growl. It does not change how she feels, it deletes the warning, and you get a dog who goes from stiff to bite with nothing in between. This is the single most dangerous thing anyone can do here.
Do not reach into the bowl, take food away, hover over her, or show her who is boss. There is no evidence hand-feeding prevents or treats food aggression, and confiscation makes it worse.
Do not run a desensitisation protocol you half remember. That is owner and professional work.
entries.why: Guarding is fear of losing something, not dominance. That is why adding value works and removing value escalates it.
entries.vet: Tell Ariel every time, and it is worth raising with the vet.

entries.title: She has given up on the puzzle toy, or she is destroying it
now: Giving up means it is too hard. Take it up without a word. Next time put half the food on top where she can simply eat it, and let her win for free for a few days.
Barking at it, biting it, flipping it over: same problem, same answer. That is frustration, not naughtiness.
Check the boring thing first. Is it sliding on a hard floor? Put it on a rug or a towel. Half of 'she cannot do it' is really 'it will not hold still'.
Is she overtired? A puppy past her nap cannot solve anything. That is a crate, not a puzzle.
Emptying it in under a minute every single time is the other kind of failure. Move up a level, or keep the level and move it to a different room.
not: Do not dig the food out for her. Make it easier next time instead. Helping teaches her to look at you the moment something is hard, which is the exact opposite of what the toy is for.
Do not leave it down once it is empty. It stops being a puzzle and becomes a chew toy, and it has a squeaker inside it.
Do not stand over her or reach into it while she is working. That is how a dog learns to guard a food toy.
Do not reach for a puzzle as the answer to a bitey evening. That is a nap.
entries.why: Frustration tolerance is something she learns, and a food puzzle is the best place to learn it, but only while she is winning most of the time. A puppy who fails at a puzzle twice stops trying at it, and that is much harder to undo than simply starting too easy.

entries.title: She is humping my leg or a cushion
now: Calmly disengage. Stand up, step away, remove the cushion.
Redirect: ask for a sit, give a chew, or move her to the pen for a short reset.
Treat it as an arousal reading. If she is humping she is over threshold, and the next thing is usually the overtired entry.
not: Do not laugh, film it, or wrestle her off. Attention of any flavour reinforces it.
Do not scold or punish her. It is normal and she has no idea what the telling-off is about.
entries.why: At ten weeks this is not sexual. Mounting appears in play from as early as three to six weeks and usually signals over-excitement or uncertainty. Because it is an arousal symptom, the fix is lowering arousal, not correcting the behavior.

entries.title: She is jumping all over people
now: Turn your back, fold your arms, no words, no eye contact. Wait for four paws on the floor.
The instant all four feet are down, turn and greet her, and put the treat on the floor between her front feet, so the reward happens where you want her body.
Better, get ahead of it: as someone approaches, start scattering treats on the floor before she thinks about launching.
Ask visitors to do exactly the same. Consistency across people is the whole game.
not: No knee in the chest, no standing on toes, no shouting. She is ten weeks old and this is a friendly greeting.
Do not just ignore it and stop there. Ignoring alone leaves a frustrated puppy with no idea what else to do. You have to pay the alternative.
entries.why: She jumps because it works. Faces are up there and jumping has produced attention before. Any attention, including a no, pays it.

entries.title: She has stolen something and will not give it back
now: Do not chase her. Chasing turns it into the best game she has ever played and multiplies what the item is worth.
Trade. Go to the fridge, make the food noise, and scatter something high value several feet away from her. When she leaves the item, pick it up calmly.
If she will not trade, open a door into another room, toss food through, close the door behind her, retrieve the item.
Then put that whole category of thing away. Socks, shoes, remotes, laundry.
not: Do not prise her mouth open or grab her collar. It teaches her to swallow fast to keep it, and it is a direct route to guarding.
Do not scold her when she finally gives it up. You would be punishing the surrender.
entries.vet: If she has actually swallowed something, that is a vet call now, not a behavior question. Do not try to make her vomit.

entries.title: She is tearing round the apartment like she is possessed
now: Let it happen. It is normal, self-limiting, usually seconds to a couple of minutes, and not a behavior problem.
Make the space safe rather than stopping her: clear the table corner, block the stairs, shut the bathroom, throw down a runner. Slick floors at speed are the real injury risk.
Move away and sit down.
When it ends, that is your window: toilet, then crate or pen with a chew. Zoomies often run straight into a crash.
not: Do not chase her. Chasing turns a thirty-second burst into a ten-minute game.
Do not grab a puppy at full speed. That is how you get a bite and a frightened dog.

entries.title: It is pouring. What do you do?
now: You still take her out. Rain does not change her bladder, and skipping trips is how you get a day full of accidents.
Change what the trip IS. Toilet trip, not a walk. Out, one spot, wait, back in. Two or three minutes. No sniffing tour.

FIND COVER. Outdoors but not under the sky: your building entrance or awning, scaffolding, a covered stoop, a doorway, the edge of a parking garage. In this city there is scaffolding on half the blocks and it is a dry corridor.
Pick one covered spot and use the same one every time. It becomes her rain spot.
Gear: a raincoat for her, and an umbrella you hold over HER, not over you. She is the one who has to relax enough to squat.
Towels by the door before you leave, not after you get back. Paws, belly, chest, then dry her properly. A damp undercoat does not care whether the water came from a tub or the sky.
Pay it enormously when she goes in the rain. Chicken, not kibble. Going in the rain is genuinely harder than going in sunshine and it should be worth more.
not: Do not skip the trip and hope. She will go indoors instead, and that is a rep that trains the floor.
Do not rush her once you are out there. Stand still and be boring. Hurrying her is what makes her hold it.
Do not drag her straight back in the second she goes, even in rain. Same rule as always: that teaches her holding it makes the outing shorter.
Do not use the balcony or a pad for ordinary rain. That teaches her a surface at home is a bathroom, and you will be undoing it for months.
entries.why: The bigger point is the timing. She is in her socialisation window until about 16 weeks, and a puppy who goes out in rain a few times now files it as normal and unremarkable for life. A dog who first meets heavy rain at eight months can decide she is not doing that, and then you have twelve years of a dog who will not toilet in bad weather. So take her out in MILD rain deliberately, before you are forced to in a downpour. It is the cheapest it will ever be.

entries.title: A real storm, where going outside is not safe
now: Lightning, or a storm severe enough that being outside is genuinely unsafe, is a different thing from rain.
For that, a pee pad indoors for that one occasion is better than her holding until she is in pain.
Put it as far from her crate and her bed as the apartment allows, and pick it up the moment the weather clears.
Take her back to the normal routine at the very next trip.
not: Do not leave the pad down afterwards. The exception stops being an exception the second it becomes furniture.
Do not do this for ordinary rain. See the rain entry.
entries.why: Expect it to cost you a little. She will be slightly more willing to go indoors afterwards, because she has now had one successful rep on an indoor surface. That is an acceptable price for a once-a-year situation and not an acceptable price for weather you could have walked her in.
entries.vet: Thunder fear is a real and common thing in dogs, and it usually gets worse with age rather than better. If she is frightened rather than just wet, mention it early: it is far more treatable at ten weeks than at three years.

entries.title: She is eating grass, leaves, mulch or another dog's poop
now: Look ahead, not down. Scan ten feet in front and steer around it before she commits. That is most of the job.
Cheerful lets-go before she reaches it, and pay her for turning her head toward you. Reward the turn away, never the approach.
Already in her mouth: do not pry her jaws or grab her collar. Produce food, step away from her, and let her come to you to trade.
Short leash around tree pits and mulch. Carry treats good enough to outbid a New York sidewalk.
not: Do not yell or lunge. Use-it-or-lose-it is exactly the lesson she takes.

Do not buy a stool-eating deterrent. Hart 2018 surveyed about 3,000 owners across all eleven products then on sale: 0 to 2 percent success. Chasing her off, 1 to 2 percent. The best of a bad field was trained leave-it at 4 percent.
entries.why: Coprophagy looks to be inherited scavenging, with no association with diet and none with how easily a dog housetrains. So she is not missing a nutrient and she does not need stricter training. It is a leash-handling problem. Grass eating separately is normal: Sueda and Hart, 1,571 dogs, about 79 percent ate grass, only about 9 percent seemed unwell first.
entries.vet: Eating other dogs' feces is a real parasite route and she is not fully vaccinated. Tell the vet.

entries.title: She is pulling on the leash
now: Front-clip harness, fixed six-foot leash. No retractable leash, and nothing attached to her collar under tension.
The moment the leash goes tight, stop walking, or turn and go the other way. Pulling never gets her closer to the thing. Loose leash restarts the walk.
Feed her continuously while she is at your side.
Keep it short. For a ten-week-old, half a block is a success, and sniffing counts as the walk.
not: Do not jerk or pop the leash. It loads her neck, she still gets to pull most of the time so it does not even work, and it pairs discomfort with whatever she was looking at. That is how leash reactivity is built.
No prong, choke or shock collar.
Do not start a head halter. It needs careful conditioning and is not for a puppy this age.
entries.why: The welfare case for a harness over a collar is strong. The claim that a front-clip harness mechanically reduces pulling better than everything else is not settled. Treat the harness as the safe default plus training, not as a fix for pulling.

entries.title: She will not come when called
now: Say her name and come once, in a high delighted voice, then run backwards away from her. Chasing makes her flee; moving away makes her chase you.
Pay every single recall, including a slow late sloppy one. Food, then a few seconds of fuss.
Keep a light line on her indoors so you never have to grab or lunge.
Practice gotcha: call, treat, take her collar, treat again. Otherwise the collar grab itself becomes the punishment.
not: Never tell her off for coming, however late. You would be punishing the arrival.
Do not call her for things she dislikes: crate, bath, nail trim, end of a walk. That poisons the word permanently. If you need her for something unpleasant, go and get her.
Do not call repeatedly in a rising voice. You teach her the word means nothing until it is shouted.

entries.title: She is terrified of something
now: Increase distance. Cross the street, step into a doorway, turn a corner. Distance is the fastest intervention there is.
Feed. While the thing is there and she is coping, deliver a stream of high-value food, and stop the second it is gone. Thing appears, chicken rains. Thing leaves, chicken stops.
Comfort her if she seeks it. You are her safe base.
Elevator: carry her, or wait for the next one. Stairs: carry her up and set her down one step from the top so she succeeds on one step, then work backwards.
not: Do not force her toward it to get her over it. That sensitises rather than desensitises and can produce panic or a bite.
Do not lure her closer with food. If she steps toward it chasing a treat and then startles, the fear gets worse. Let her pick the distance.
Do not scold her for being frightened.
Do not believe that comforting her reinforces the fear. That is a myth. Fear is an emotion and reinforcement acts on behavior.
entries.why: Her socialization window closes around sixteen weeks. Every scary encounter right now is being written down, which is the argument for retreating today rather than pushing through.

entries.title: She will not move outside. She has planted herself
now: Stop pulling. Put slack in the leash. Wait, and count to thirty.
Crouch or move away from her, sideways, and sound cheerful. Puppies follow movement away and brace against pressure toward them.
Toss a treat a foot in front of her and let her walk to it herself. Pay any movement at all, including one step.
Still stuck: carry her. Better, carry her a short way from home and set her down facing home, so walking is now what she wants.
not: Do not drag her, not even a little. It loads her neck, she cannot be reasoned with, and it pairs the street with being overpowered.
Do not make carrying the first move every time or you teach a very effective way to end a walk.
Do not push through it so she gets used to it. Forced exposure makes fear worse, not better.
entries.why: Two different causes, same look. Overwhelmed or frightened, or simply finished, because she is ten weeks old. Either way the answer is the same: release pressure, reduce the demand, go home.

entries.title: She panics when I leave the room
now: Practice absences while you are home. Pen her in the kitchen while you are next door, so confinement does not only ever predict your departure.
Build duration from tiny. One or two minutes, then longer over days.
Leave with a stuffed frozen Kong. Leave and come back low-key: no emotional goodbye, no big greeting.
Never punish her for anything you find when you get back.
not: Do not make a fuss on departure and a bigger fuss on arrival.
Do not force a genuinely panicking puppy into a shut crate. For some dogs the crate adds stress. Use a baby-gated room instead.
entries.why: Normal puppy distress settles over minutes and improves over days. True separation anxiety happens specifically and only when she is alone: anxiety as you get ready to leave, destruction aimed at doors and windows, soiling only when alone, refusing food when alone. That is a clinical condition diagnosed by a vet and a veterinary behaviorist. Report what you saw, do not run a programme.
entries.vet: If it looks like the second description, that is a vet conversation.

entries.title: She will not settle for me and I am not her owner
now: Keep Ariel's routine exactly. Same feeding times, same last toilet, same bedtime, same crate in the same spot. Predictability is most of the job.
Put an unwashed t-shirt of his in the crate. Add one of yours if you will be there several days.
Be boring. Do not lean over her, reach for her, stare, or scoop her up. Sit on the floor sideways and let her come to you.
Hand-feed her and deliver every meal and chew yourself. That is the fastest legitimate route to being safe to be around.
not: Do not try to win her over with intensity: picking her up, following her, high-pitched cooing. Social pressure from a stranger raises arousal in a puppy who is already unsettled.
Do not loosen the rules out of sympathy. She's stressed so she can sleep on the sofa tonight breaks the routine that is holding her together and hands Ariel a new problem.

entries.title: Is the apartment too hot or too cold for her?
now: 69F is right and needs no adjusting. It is the exact figure the Merck Veterinary Manual gives for a puppy from week five, and it sits inside the range where she is not spending energy heating or cooling herself.
One setting all day. There is no evidence for different temperatures for sleeping, resting and play, and anyone giving you three numbers is inventing them.

Keep her crate away from the radiator. Old steam radiators run far hotter than the thermostat and create a pocket the wall reading cannot see. Put a thermometer inside the crate for a night rather than trusting the wall.
Manage play, not the room. Around three quarters of heat illness in dogs is caused by exercise, not hot weather. She will not self-limit, so you enforce breaks.
not: Do not lower the thermostat because she pants during play. Fix the play.
Do not assume a covered crate is neutral. It cuts airflow while she is producing heat and moisture, and nobody has measured what that does. Cover partially, use something woven, measure it once.
Do not rely on shivering as your cold signal. It stops as hypothermia deepens, so she is not shivering so she is fine is bad logic.
entries.why: Goldens are double-coated and had 2.65 times the odds of heat illness compared with Labradors across 905,000 UK dogs. Worth knowing the caveat: coat type was not actually measured in that study, so the undercoat is the proposed explanation rather than a tested one. Either way, erring cool suits her.
entries.vet: Panting at rest in a 69F room with no exercise beforehand is not normal. Nor is stopping mid-play, which is the sign people miss.

entries.title: Where the bowls go, and how to stop her tipping them
now: FOOD: one place only. The kitchen. One spot, one container, so three people cannot lose track of how much she has had.
WATER: as many places as she spends time. One in the kitchen, one wherever she actually lies down. Two bowls is completely normal and there is no downside.
A bowl she has to walk to another room for is a bowl she drinks less from. Puppies do not get up to travel for a drink, especially if they are comfortable near you.
Heavy stainless steel or ceramic with a wide flat base. Weight beats a puppy.
A rubber mat or a boot tray underneath. It will not stop a spill but it stops the mess.
At 8pm pick up ALL the water bowls, not just one, or she will simply go and drink from the other.
not: No water bowl in the crate for normal naps or overnight. She does not need it for a short stretch, and it is what causes the spills.
No light plastic bowls. She will flip them, and scratched plastic harbours bacteria and is linked to puppy chin acne.
entries.why: The two are different problems. Food needs structure because it is measured and because three people are feeding her. Water needs no structure at all, because nobody is counting it.

entries.title: How much can she have? The 10 percent rule
now: No more than about 70 to 100 kcal a day from anything that is not her complete-and-balanced food. That is roughly 10 percent of her intake.
That budget is SHARED between the three of you. Not 10 percent each. This is the most common way a puppy ends up overfed.

The whole day of treats is ONE of these: about 60 to 80 pieces of her own kibble, OR 3 baby carrots plus 5 blueberries plus a quarter cup of apple, OR one inch-cube of chicken plus half a cup of green beans, OR 2 teaspoons of peanut butter and nothing else all day.
Judge her by body condition, not by the chart. Aim for 4 out of 9: ribs easily felt, visible waist from above, tuck from the side.
not: Do not free-feed. Measure every meal.

Do not treat "she is still hungry" as evidence that she needs more. Golden retrievers carry a documented appetite-drive gene variant. Hunger in this breed is a poor guide to requirement. Use the scale and the ribs.
Do not read a visible waist on a golden puppy as neglect. It is correct.
entries.why: Kealy 1992 is the strongest single piece of evidence in this whole guide. Forty-eight Labradors from 8 weeks old, randomised: one group fed freely, one fed 25 percent less of the same food, followed for life with serial hip X-rays. Hip dysplasia appeared in 7 of 24 limit-fed dogs versus 16 of 24 fed freely. Same food, same breed, only the amount differed. The restricted group also developed arthritis later and lived longer.
entries.vet: Ask your vet to show you how to body condition score her, and to weigh her at every visit.

entries.title: What to actually buy: the four tests
now: SOFT. Press your thumbnail into it. If you cannot leave a dent, it is too hard for her teeth. At this age it should squash between finger and thumb.
TINY. Pea-sized, or breakable into pea-sized pieces. A training session is 20 to 40 repetitions, and each reward has to be nearly free.
SHORT INGREDIENT LIST. Not for purity reasons, but because if she reacts you need to know what she reacted to. A treat with 14 ingredients is uninterpretable.
LOW CALORIE. Aim for 2 kcal a piece or less, so a full session costs under 40 kcal.
Plus, for her specifically: no added calcium, no bone meal, no bone-and-joint blends, no fortified multivitamin treats.
Good buys now: soft training treats broken into quarters, her own kibble, a Kong Puppy, frozen blueberries and watermelon, a snuffle mat or lick mat filled from her ration.
not: Do not buy dental chews. She has no adult teeth to clean, and most fail the thumbnail test.
Do not buy jerky treats. There is an open FDA investigation into illnesses linked to them.

Be careful with freeze-dried RAW treats. Freeze-drying does not sterilize, and FDA sampling found roughly a one in three hit rate for foodborne pathogens in raw pet products bought online. For an unvaccinated puppy in a three-adult household, prefer cooked or dehydrated. Wash hands either way.
Liver is very rich in vitamin A and copper. A few crumbs a day, not a handful.
entries.why: Her 28 baby teeth are needle-sharp but thin-walled, with a large pulp chamber and very little enamel. They are built for nursing and mouthing, not load-bearing chewing, and under pressure they crack. A fractured baby tooth can damage the adult tooth bud growing underneath it. She also cannot shear yet, she gulps, which is the core obstruction risk behind every no in this section.

entries.title: Why she must never have a calcium supplement
now: Zero calcium supplements. No bone meal, no eggshell powder, no puppy bone-builder, no multivitamin, no joint blend, unless her vet specifically prescribes one.
No treats fortified with calcium or marketed for bone and joint support.
Keep dairy small and occasional. Cottage cheese and yogurt are calcium.
Her food should carry the AAFCO statement for growth INCLUDING large-size dogs, 70 lb or more as an adult. That exact phrase. A food can say it is for growth and still not be right for her.
not: Do not add plain meat on top of her food thinking it is healthier. Meat is phosphorus-rich and calcium-poor, so it skews the ratio the other way. Both directions of the ratio cause harm.
Do not assume more calcium builds stronger bones. In a large-breed puppy it damages the growth plate.
entries.why: Adult dogs turn down calcium absorption when there is too much in the diet. Puppies under 6 months cannot: the gut passively absorbs about 70 percent of whatever calcium is present, with no off-switch. Excess calcium suppresses bone remodelling and disrupts the orderly conversion of cartilage to bone at the growth plate, which is the exact lesion behind osteochondrosis. This was demonstrated experimentally in Great Danes fed diets differing only in calcium. Goldens are already one of the highest-prevalence breeds for hip and elbow dysplasia. Diet will not override her genes, but it can change whether a susceptible dog expresses the disease. Over-supplementing is the far more common and far more dangerous error; true deficiency is nearly impossible on a complete commercial food.
entries.vet: Ask whether her current food is appropriate for large-breed growth, and ask for the calcium and phosphorus figures on a dry-matter basis. The guaranteed analysis on the bag gives only a calcium MINIMUM, which tells you nothing about excess.

entries.title: The one-container rule, for three people
now: Measure the whole day of food into ONE container each morning.
Meals come out of it. Training rewards come out of it. The Kong is filled from it.
When the container is empty, she has had her food for the day.
Anything that is NOT from the container gets written down: date, item, amount, who gave it, and her stool the next day.
not: Do not let three people each decide independently what "a little bit" means.
entries.why: Three people each giving just a little bit is exactly how a large-breed puppy ends up 25 percent over target with a diluted mineral profile, and how a food reaction becomes impossible to trace. One container removes the arithmetic entirely. It also means nobody has to remember whether someone else already fed her.

entries.title: Water in the crate, if she is in there a long stretch
now: For normal naps and overnight, no water in the crate. She does not need it.
If she is crated a couple of hours or more, or it is a hot day, she does need water in there.
Use a CLIP-ON bowl. Stainless steel, hooks onto the crate bars, off the floor. She cannot tip it because it is fixed to the side of the crate. A few dollars, and it is what most people use.
Or a spouted water bottle that clips to the bars, like a rabbit bottle but dog-sized. Zero spill. Some dogs take a day to work out the spout.
The clip-on bowl is the easier of the two. Start there.
not: Do not put a loose bowl on the crate floor. She will knock it over, soak the bedding, and then you have a wet puppy and a wash load.
entries.why: A soaked crate is not just a mess. Damp bedding overnight is uncomfortable, and a crate that is regularly wet stops being a place she wants to be, which undermines the crate training.

entries.title: Introducing anything new: one thing, three days
now: One new item at a time. Three clear days before the next one. Written down.
Start with a token amount. One blueberry. One pea-sized piece of chicken. Not a portion.
The three-day clock is shared across all three of you, which is why it only works if it is written somewhere all of you can see.

Watch: stool consistency and color (12 to 48 hours), mucus or blood (12 to 48 hours), vomiting (2 to 12 hours), gas and gurgling (4 to 24 hours), itching and paw licking (hours to days), appetite and energy (24 hours).
If anything is off, stop everything new and wait for two clear days before restarting.

Changing her actual food: 75/25 for two days, 50/50 for two days, 25/75 for three days, then 100 percent. Puppies often need 14 days. If stool loosens, hold at the current ratio for two or three extra days rather than going backwards.
not: Do not advance a food transition and add a new treat on the same day.
Do not give pumpkin to firm up her stool while you are still trying to work out what caused it.
entries.why: The reason for this rule is not that carrots are dangerous. It is that right now, if she produces a loose stool, there are at least six live explanations and you cannot tell them apart: the ongoing food transition, something new someone gave her, residual parasites after the Panacur course, something she scavenged on a walk, stress from the move, or parvovirus. Every new food you add makes that list longer and your diagnosis worse. She is not fully vaccinated, and parvo is the one you cannot afford to miss.
entries.vet: Book her post-deworming fecal recheck. Standard practice is 2 to 4 weeks after the course.

entries.title: Can leftovers be used as treats later?
now: Yes, under three conditions.
One: portion it off BEFORE the bowl goes down to her. Once she has eaten from it, it is finished.
Two: refrigerate at 40F or below in a sealed, labelled container. Rehydrated kibble 24 hours. Opened gently-cooked 3 days.
Three: once it leaves the fridge, the 2 hour clock applies, or 1 hour above 90F. Take out only what you will use in one session.
Best routine: each morning, portion the day into a meal container and a small training container. Freeze the rest of an opened pouch in ice cube trays for Kongs. Date-label everything.
not: Do not scrape her bowl back into the container.
Do not carry gently-cooked food around in a treat pouch all day.
entries.why: This is the right instinct and it solves two problems at once. It stops you wasting a 9 oz pouch, and food she ignores in a bowl she will often work hard for by hand. Food out of a bowl and food out of your hand are different currencies to a puppy.

entries.title: How long does her food last? Bowl, fridge, freezer
now: Rehydrated bowl at room temperature: 2 hours is the absolute maximum. In practice, pick it up after 20 to 30 minutes.
NYC in summer with no AC: 1 hour maximum. Above 90F the safe window halves.
A bowl she has already eaten from: do not refrigerate and re-serve. Throw the remainder away. Her saliva reseeds it.
Opened gently-cooked pouch, refrigerated in a sealed labelled container: 3 days. That is the manufacturer number and it is stricter than general guidance, so use it.
Rehydrated kibble made ahead and never served, refrigerated: 24 hours.
Gently-cooked food in a treat pouch on your hip: 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90F. Be strict about this one.
Frozen in portions or stuffed Kongs: 3 to 4 months. Thaw in the fridge, never on the counter.
Opened dry kibble bag: about 6 weeks. Keep it in its original bag, rolled and clipped, INSIDE an airtight container.
Wash bowls and scoops daily in hot soapy water.
not: Do not leave the bowl down all morning. Warm water starts the food inside the bacterial danger zone rather than having to fall into it, so the clock is already running the moment you put it down.
Do not pour kibble loose into a storage container. The bag is a barrier layer and it carries the lot code you would need in a recall, and residual fats go rancid on the container walls.
Do not keep a scratched plastic bowl. Scratches harbour bacteria and are linked to puppy chin acne.
entries.why: The moment you add warm water to kibble and mix in cooked meat, you have made a moist, protein-rich, neutral-pH medium sitting in the bacterial danger zone between 40F and 140F, where bacteria can double in number every 20 minutes. USDA guidance is 2 hours out of refrigeration, or 1 hour above 90F. Dry kibble is a completely different object: low water activity, stable. The rehydrated bowl is not.
entries.vet: If she has repeated loose stool and the bowl has been sitting down for hours, mention the timings.

entries.title: Water: always down, except after 8pm
now: Water bowl full and available all day. Top it up when it gets low.
Never limit water to control her peeing. A puddle on the floor is not a problem. A dried-out puppy is.
The one limit: pick the bowl up at 8pm, two hours before her 10pm bedtime. That is so she does not fill up right before sleeping.
If she is clearly thirsty after 8pm, give her a small drink anyway, then take her straight out. Never leave her thirsty to keep the crate clean.
Wash the bowls daily in hot soapy water. Bowls build a film.
not: Do NOT pick the water up early if it is hot, if she has been running around, if she has been sick or had runny stools, if she is on any medicine, or if she just seems off. On those days leave water down all night.
Do not measure water. Food gets measured; water does not.
Do not put a normal bowl in the crate. She will tip it. See the bowls entry.
entries.why: Free water actually makes her toilet schedule MORE predictable, not less. With water always there she takes small sips through the day, so it is small sips in and small pees out on a steady rhythm. If water is only there sometimes she gets thirsty, and when the bowl appears she gulps a large amount at once, then urgently needs to go twenty minutes later. Thirsty puppy, big drink, surprise puddle. That is what wrecks a schedule. And at ten weeks she needs to go out every hour or two regardless; her bladder size is what drives that, not the water bowl.
entries.vet: Drinking a lot more than usual, day after day and not just after a walk, is a vet call. So is refusing to drink at all, same day. Check her gums: press a finger on them, they should feel wet and slippery. Sticky or dry means she needs water and she needs a vet.

entries.title: Alcohol
entries.line: A 6 kg puppy has essentially no reserve.
entries.prep: Non-obvious sources: raw dough, rum cake, sangria fruit, hand sanitiser, mouthwash, fermenting trash, some liquid medicines.
entries.why: Low blood sugar and low body temperature are what kill, not the intoxication itself.

entries.title: Antlers, elk and deer
entries.line: Never, at any age.
entries.prep: Thumbnail test: press your thumbnail into it. If you cannot leave a dent, it is too hard for her teeth. No antler passes.
entries.why: Antler evolved to survive being hit by another antler. It is among the most common causes of slab fracture of the carnassial tooth, and no board-certified veterinary dentist endorses them. They also splinter.

entries.title: Apple
entries.line: Yes, with the core and seeds out.
entries.amount: A quarter cup chopped, about 15 kcal.
entries.prep: Core and seeds removed. Cut into pea-sized pieces, not slices.
entries.why: The seed question, honestly: apple seeds do contain a cyanide precursor, but you would need hundreds of crushed seeds, and a few swallowed whole pass straight through. The real reason to take the core out is that the core is a choking and obstruction object for a 6 kg puppy. Mechanical, not chemical.

entries.title: Avocado
entries.line: Not at her age. The reason is mechanical, not chemical.
entries.prep: Guacamole is a hard no at any age, because of the onion and garlic.
entries.why: Sources genuinely disagree here. The ASPCA lists avocado to avoid; Merck and Pet Poison Helpline say dogs are relatively resistant to persin. What everyone agrees on is that the pit is a perfect obstruction size for a puppy and the fat load is wrong for a gut still on a food transition.
entries.age: Plain ripe flesh in small amounts is low risk from around 6 months, but nutritionally pointless.

entries.title: Banana
entries.line: Yes, small amounts.
entries.amount: An eighth of a cup mashed, about 25 kcal. A coin-thick slice or two.
entries.prep: Peel off. The peel is indigestible and an obstruction risk.
entries.why: High sugar for the calories. Excellent Kong filler because it is sticky.

entries.title: Blueberries
entries.line: Yes. The best fresh training treat on this list.
entries.amount: Three to five berries, about 2 to 3 kcal.
entries.prep: Fresh or thawed. Whole is fine, they are soft and compressible.
entries.why: Frozen ones are a good teething soother.

entries.title: Bully sticks
entries.line: Not yet. Commonly given from around 6 months, with three caveats.
entries.amount: Measured at 9 to 22 kcal per inch. An average 6 inch stick is 88 kcal, which is her entire daily treat budget in one chew.
entries.prep: If you ever use one, use a bully stick holder and confiscate it at about 3 inches. No exceptions.
entries.why: Three separate problems. The end becomes a swallowable obstruction object. The calories are enormous. And in a Tufts study of 26 sticks, one carried C. difficile, one carried MRSA, and seven carried E. coli, so wash your hands. Honest note: the 6 month figure is convention, not data. There is no age that makes a swallowable object safe.
entries.age: Around 6 months at the earliest, with a holder.

entries.title: Coffee, tea, energy drinks
entries.line: Same thresholds as chocolate. About one small cup of coffee is enough to cause signs.
entries.prep: Used coffee grounds and tea bags in an open kitchen trash can are the real-world exposure. Keep the lid shut.
entries.why: Also in pre-workout scoops, caffeine tablets and diet pills.

entries.title: Cannabis and THC edibles
entries.line: A genuine NYC sidewalk hazard. Emergency.
entries.prep: Edibles usually pair THC with chocolate and sometimes xylitol, so it is often a triple exposure.
entries.why: Puppies are severely affected at small doses.
entries.signs: Wobbliness, dribbling urine, low body temperature, slow heart rate, glazed staring.

entries.title: Carrot
entries.line: Yes, but not as a whole raw chew yet.
entries.amount: One baby carrot is 3 to 4 kcal.
entries.prep: Cut into coins, or steam until it yields. Do not hand her a whole raw carrot.
entries.why: A whole raw carrot is a swallowable cylinder for a puppy who gulps rather than shears. Fine as a chew from around 4 to 5 months, once the adult premolars are in.

entries.title: Cheese
entries.line: Yes but tightly capped. Calorie density is the problem, not toxicity.
entries.amount: One 1 cm cube is about 12 kcal. Maximum one to two cubes a day.
entries.prep: Plain hard cheese only. Never blue cheese, which contains a tremorgenic toxin. Never garlic or herb. Never processed slices.
entries.why: Very high value for training and very calorie-dense, plus high fat and sodium. Fine as an occasional jackpot, not as a routine treat. Hard cheeses like cheddar and parmesan are lower in lactose and better tolerated than soft.

entries.title: Plain cooked chicken or turkey
entries.line: Yes. Your best high-value training treat.
entries.amount: One 1 cm cube is about 15 kcal. Three to five cubes a day at most.
entries.prep: Boiled or baked. Skinless, boneless, no seasoning of any kind. Never deli meat, never rotisserie, never the skin.
entries.why: Shred it to pea size for training, so a session of 20 repetitions costs about 10 kcal. Rotisserie chicken rub contains onion and garlic powder; deli meat is loaded with sodium and nitrates.

entries.title: Chocolate and cocoa
entries.line: Dose matters, and darker is far worse.
entries.amount: For her size: roughly 2 g of baking chocolate, 10 g of dark, or 24 g of milk chocolate is enough to start causing signs.
entries.prep: Cocoa mulch on planters counts. So does hot chocolate powder.
entries.why: Theobromine and caffeine, which dogs clear very slowly. White chocolate is not meaningfully toxic but is a fat and sugar load.
entries.signs: Vomiting, restlessness, racing heart, tremors, seizures. Onset 6 to 12 hours.

entries.title: Cooked bones of any kind
entries.line: Never, at any age. No credible source disagrees.
entries.prep: NYC-specific: discarded cooked chicken and rib bones on the sidewalk are the single most common street scavenge hazard. Leave it and drop it are the two highest-value things you can teach her this month.
entries.why: They splinter into sharp shards. The FDA logged around 90 illnesses and 15 deaths from commercial bone treats between 2010 and 2017: perforation, obstruction, tooth fracture, rectal bleeding.
entries.signs: Retching, vomiting after drinking, painful belly, straining with no stool. Surgical emergency.

entries.title: Corn cobs
entries.line: Never. This is the one vets pull out of dogs most often.
entries.prep: Trash can lid shut, always. Summer barbecues, park trash cans and street food are the exposure.
entries.why: ASPCA Animal Hospital vets name the corn cob as the single most common foreign body they surgically remove from dogs. It is exactly the wrong size and diameter to pass, it does not break down, and it does not always show clearly on X-ray.
entries.signs: Repeated retching, vomiting after drinking, refusing food, painful belly, no stool. Surgical emergency.

entries.title: Cucumber
entries.line: Yes. Near-zero calories.
entries.amount: A few thin half-moons.
entries.prep: Cut rounds in half so they cannot sit flat over the airway.
entries.why: A good hot-weather treat that costs almost nothing against her budget.

entries.title: Raw bread dough
entries.line: Dangerous in small amounts, by two mechanisms at once.
entries.amount: A small ball of dough is disproportionately dangerous in a small stomach.
