entries.prep: Baked bread is not this hazard. It is just calories.
entries.why: The dough rises in the warm stomach and distends it like bloat, cutting off blood supply to the stomach wall. At the same time the yeast ferments into alcohol, which is absorbed into her bloodstream.
entries.signs: Retching with nothing coming up, swollen belly, then wobbliness and disorientation.

entries.title: Egg
entries.line: Yes, fully cooked.
entries.amount: A quarter of a large cooked egg, about 18 kcal. Cap at a quarter egg a day.
entries.prep: Scrambled with no butter, oil or salt, or hard-boiled. Never raw. No shell.
entries.why: Very useful for a picky eater.

entries.title: Grapes, raisins, currants, sultanas
entries.line: Treat any amount as an emergency. There is no known safe dose.
entries.amount: The rule of thumb is one grape or raisin per 10 lb of body weight may be enough. For her, that is one or two.
entries.prep: Also hiding in: raisin bread, trail mix, granola bars, oatmeal cookies, fruitcake, Raisin Bran, cream of tartar, grape juice.
entries.why: Tartaric acid, which dogs excrete poorly, damages the kidneys. Content varies hugely between grapes, which is why some dogs eat a bunch and are fine and others go into kidney failure on a handful. That variability is exactly why there is no safe dose.
entries.signs: Vomiting within hours, then kidney failure over about 72 hours.

entries.title: Green beans
entries.line: Yes.
entries.amount: Half a cup boiled is about 22 kcal.
entries.prep: Plain, no salt. Cut each bean in half at this age; a whole one is a swallowable string.
entries.why: Fresh or frozen plain. Never canned with salt, never green bean casserole, which contains onion.

entries.title: Hooves
entries.line: Never.
entries.why: Same fracture risk as antler, plus they split into sharp curved shards that lodge across the palate or perforate the gut.

entries.title: Ice cubes
entries.line: Fine, with a caveat, and not worth arguing about.
entries.prep: Crushed ice or shavings are the safer version.
entries.why: The claim that ice cracks teeth is repeated everywhere with almost no evidence behind it. Ice does fail the thumbnail test, but it shatters rather than resisting.

entries.title: Kong Puppy (stuffable rubber)
entries.line: The single best thing you can buy her right now.
entries.amount: Size Small or Extra Small.
entries.prep: Get the PUPPY Kong, the blue or pink one, not the red Classic. The puppy rubber is softer and made for 2 to 9 month old mouths.
entries.why: Passes the thumbnail test, no fracture risk, nothing to swallow. Stuff it with her own soaked kibble mash and freeze it: that is a 20 minute enrichment activity, a teething soother and a crate-training tool, all funded from her measured ration rather than from her treat budget. Check it regularly and throw it away if pieces come off.

entries.title: Seasoned human food and leftovers
entries.line: The realistic poisoning risk in this apartment is not a raw onion. It is your dinner.
entries.prep: Onion and garlic powder are in almost all savoury leftovers: gravy, stock, soup, pizza, Chinese takeaway, rotisserie chicken skin and rub, hummus, most commercial broths, baby food.
entries.why: People check for chocolate and never check for garlic powder, and it is in nearly everything savoury.

entries.title: Macadamia nuts
entries.line: A very low threshold. Roughly two to six nuts is enough for her.
entries.amount: Signs documented from 0.7 g per kg. A single nut weighs 2 to 3 g.
entries.prep: They usually arrive inside chocolate or cookies, so it tends to be a double exposure.
entries.why: Mechanism unknown. Usually resolves in 24 to 48 hours, but the presentation is frightening.
entries.signs: Hind legs give way, unable to stand, tremors, vomiting, fever. Within 12 hours.

entries.title: Mouldy food and compost
entries.line: Small amounts are enough.
entries.prep: Trash can lid shut. This includes mouldy bread, cheese and nuts.
entries.why: Tremorgenic mycotoxins.

entries.title: Wild mushrooms
entries.line: Never let her mouth a mushroom, at any amount.
entries.prep: They come up in tree pits and park grass after rain, which is exactly where she sniffs.
entries.why: Some Amanita species cause fatal liver failure, and you cannot identify them on sight.

entries.title: Nutmeg
entries.line: Large amounts only. A dusting on pie is not a poisoning; eating the jar is.
entries.why: Honest note: the doses quoted online are extrapolated from human toxicology, not dog studies. Cinnamon in cooking amounts is not toxic either. Both are still off-limits now as unnecessary novelty, and the pie itself is a bigger problem for sugar and fat.
entries.signs: Disorientation, racing heart, abdominal pain, possible seizures. Onset 3 to 6 hours, can last 48.

entries.title: Whole nuts of any kind
entries.line: Not recommended at any age.
entries.prep: Nut butters, xylitol-checked, are the safe form.
entries.why: Choking size, very high fat, usually salted. Macadamia is outright toxic. Mouldy walnuts carry tremorgenic mycotoxins.

entries.title: Nylon and hard plastic chews
entries.line: No at this age, and hard grades never.
entries.prep: Only the softest puppy grades, supervised, thrown away at the first sign of chunking.
entries.why: Two hazards. Hard grades fracture teeth. And swallowed shards do not show up on a plain X-ray, which makes an obstruction much harder to diagnose.

entries.title: Onion, garlic, leek, chive, shallot
entries.line: Never, and it builds up. Powders are worse than fresh.
entries.amount: Garlic is three to five times more toxic than onion by weight.
entries.prep: Cooking, drying and powdering do not destroy it. This is why every cooked-food entry here insists on plain and unseasoned.
entries.why: Destroys red blood cells. The catch is the timing: she can look completely fine for several days and then become anaemic.
entries.signs: Days later: weakness, pale gums, dark urine, jaundice, collapse. Do not assume she got away with it because day one was fine.

entries.title: Other safe vegetables and fruit
entries.line: Also fine now, same rules: plain, pea-sized, one new thing at a time.
entries.amount: Boiled courgette three quarters of a cup 28 kcal. Baked butternut squash quarter cup 21 kcal. Boiled spinach half a cup 21 kcal. One strawberry 4 kcal. Raw pear, seeds out. Honeydew.
entries.prep: Plain air-popped popcorn is fine by calories but skip it at this age, because unpopped kernels are a choking risk.
entries.why: Skip spinach if she ever has urinary problems, because of the oxalates. Applesauce, honey and marshmallows are just sugar for a growing puppy and are not worth it.

entries.title: Peanut butter
entries.line: Yes, AFTER you read the label. Every jar, every time.
entries.amount: A teaspoon is about 30 kcal, which is a third of her entire daily treat budget.
entries.prep: Check for xylitol or birch sugar on every single jar. Unsalted, unsweetened, ideally 100 percent peanuts.
entries.why: Best used as a thin smear inside a Kong, not spooned. A pea-sized amount is plenty. Peanut butter is also the standard way people hide pills, which is exactly why a xylitol jar in the cupboard is unusually dangerous.

entries.title: Plain pumpkin puree
entries.line: Yes, capped at a tablespoon a day.
entries.amount: A teaspoon is about 2 kcal, a tablespoon about 5.
entries.prep: Must be 100 percent pumpkin puree, NOT pumpkin pie filling. Pie filling has sugar, nutmeg, cinnamon and sometimes xylitol.
entries.why: The claim that it fixes loose stool is plausible but barely studied. More importantly: do not use it to mask diarrhea during a food transition. You need to see her real stool.

entries.title: Rat bait and rodenticide
entries.line: Emergency, and the timing is deceptive.
entries.prep: NYC-specific: bait stations sit in tree pits, basements and behind trash cans all over the city. Look before she sniffs.
entries.why: The anticoagulant types cause internal bleeding three to five days later. She can seem completely normal in between.
entries.signs: Delayed: pale gums, weakness, bruising, breathlessness. Do not wait for signs. Call immediately after any suspected contact.

entries.title: Raw meat, raw egg, raw fish
entries.line: Not while she is 10 weeks old with an incomplete vaccine series.
entries.prep: Her gently cooked food IS cooked. This entry is about extras.
entries.why: Salmonella, Listeria and Campylobacter, which are a risk to her and to the three people handling her. Raw egg white also binds biotin.

entries.title: Raw and marrow bones
entries.line: The honest recommendation is no, at any age.
entries.why: Sources disagree. Veterinary dentists and the FDA advise against all bones: slab fracture of the upper carnassial is the classic injury, plus marrow bones getting stuck around the lower jaw, plus Salmonella. Raw-feeding advocates argue soft raw bones are fine under supervision. There is no controlled trial either way. The fracture risk is documented; the claimed dental benefit is not. With an incompletely vaccinated puppy and three handlers of different experience, no is the right call.

entries.title: Rawhide
entries.line: No now, and marginal at any age.
entries.why: Swallowed chunks swell up to about four times their size in the stomach. Plus choking on the softened end, bacterial contamination, and chemical processing residues. Some vets accept it for dogs that shred rather than gulp, correctly sized and supervised. A 10 week old puppy is a gulper by definition. The AKC openly acknowledges that vets are split on this one.

entries.title: Salt, salt dough, play dough
entries.line: Including craft salt dough and children play dough.
entries.why: Too much sodium causes vomiting, tremors and seizures.

entries.title: Sticks from the park
entries.line: No.
entries.why: Penetrating injuries to the mouth and throat, plus splinters. And NYC tree pits are treated with rodenticide.

entries.title: Peach, plum, cherry and avocado stones
entries.line: Never. Obstruction is the real risk, not cyanide.
entries.prep: Never leave stone fruit waste accessible. The flesh with the stone removed is fine in small amounts from a few months.
entries.why: Exactly the right size and hardness to lodge in a puppy intestine, and hard enough to fracture teeth. The cyanogenic compounds in the kernel are a secondary and far less likely concern.

entries.title: Tennis balls
entries.line: Supervised only, and correctly sized.
entries.prep: Use a rubber ball too large to fit fully in her mouth.
entries.why: The fuzz is abrasive and wears teeth down over years, and a compressed ball can spring open in the throat.

entries.title: Watermelon
entries.line: Yes, deseeded and without rind.
entries.amount: Half a cup diced is about 23 kcal.
entries.prep: Seeds and rind removed. The rind is an obstruction risk.
entries.why: Frozen chunks are good for teething.

entries.title: Xylitol / birch sugar
entries.line: The most dangerous thing on this list. An emergency at a tiny dose.
entries.amount: About 640 mg is enough to crash her blood sugar. One piece of sugar-free gum can hold 300 mg to 1 g. One or two pieces is an emergency.
entries.prep: Read the ingredient panel of every peanut butter jar, every time, before it goes near a Kong.
entries.why: Causes a huge insulin release and profound low blood sugar that can last more than 24 hours. Higher doses destroy the liver 24 to 48 hours later. Also hides in: sugar-free mints and baked goods, chewable vitamins, melatonin gummies, toothpaste, mouthwash, nasal spray, protein bars, some liquid medicines.
entries.signs: Vomiting, lethargy, wobbliness, collapse, seizures. Can start within 30 minutes.

entries.title: Yak and Himalayan cheese chews
entries.line: Not now, and honestly still marginal later.
entries.prep: If you use one at all, puff the end in the microwave and let it cool completely first.
entries.why: Very hard when dry and usually fails the thumbnail test, so tooth fracture is the risk. Also concentrated dairy and calorie-dense. The nub left at the end is a classic obstruction object.

entries.title: Plain yogurt
entries.line: Technically fine, but wait. Not a good idea this month.
entries.amount: A teaspoon is about 3 kcal. Cap at a teaspoon a day if you use it at all.
entries.prep: Plain, whole-milk, unsweetened. Check for xylitol in anything labelled light or sugar-free.
entries.why: Dogs have limited lactase and dairy is a common cause of loose stool. Right now, with a food transition and a recent Panacur course, added dairy mostly muddies your stool signal. Realistically wait until 4 to 5 months. The probiotic claim for supermarket yogurt is weakly evidenced; a veterinary probiotic is the better tool if one is actually needed.

entries.title: Will she get sick if she is not totally dry? And the air conditioning
now: Turn the air conditioning off, or well up, before the bath starts. Leave it off until she is dry to the skin.
Keep her out of any direct airflow while she is damp: AC vent, fan, open window, doorway draft.
Bathe in a warm room, at least 72F. Warm the towels first if you can.
Dry her properly rather than fast. Part the coat and touch the skin at the neck, under the elbows, chest, base of the tail and behind the ears. Cool skin or damp roots means keep going.

If she does get chilled: dry towels, a warm room, a blanket, let her curl up. Do not use a hairdryer on heat, a hot water bottle or a heat pad on her, and do not put her in warm water. Warming a cold puppy too fast is its own problem.
Watch for shivering. That is her telling you she is losing heat, and it is the signal to stop and dry her.
not: Do not let her out onto a balcony or into a hallway while damp.
Do not take her outside for one to two hours after a bath, longer in winter.
Do not leave her in a crate with a fan or a dryer aimed at it. Ever, at home or at a groomer. Dogs have died of heat stroke in cage dryers.
Do not assume the surface tells you anything. A double coat feels dry on top long before the undercoat is.
entries.why: Being wet does not give her a cold. Colds and kennel cough come from viruses and bacteria, not from temperature, and a damp dog in a warm room is not catching anything. So the honest answer to will she get sick is: not in the way you are picturing. There are two real risks though, and they are different from each other. CHILLING is a heat problem: she is small, she has a lot of surface area for her body mass and not much fat, and evaporating water pulls heat off her fast. Moving cold air makes it much faster, which is exactly what an AC vent is. That is why the AC matters and a still warm room does not. THE DAMP COAT is a skin problem: moisture trapped under a dense double coat is how acute moist dermatitis starts, which is what a hot spot is, and dense-coated breeds get them most. That is the one that is genuinely caused by leaving her not quite dry, and it shows up as a red, wet, painful patch that appears fast and that she will not leave alone. One more term, since it comes up: hypothermia is too cold, hyperthermia is too hot. She is at risk of the first from a cold draft while wet, and of the second from a hot dryer or a hot car, never from both at once.
entries.vet: A red, wet, painful patch that appeared within a day and that she keeps licking or chewing is a hot spot: same-day call, they spread fast. Shivering that does not stop once she is dry and warm, or a puppy who goes limp, weak or unusually quiet after getting cold, is also a call.

entries.title: Drying a double coat, and why it is the step that matters most
now: Press and blot with towels. Do not rub. Rubbing tangles a double coat and makes mats.
Expect to use three or four towels. Swap as soon as one is saturated.
A cool-air canine dryer is the right tool. If you use a human hairdryer: COOL or lowest setting only, never the heat setting, at least 12 inches away, kept constantly moving.
Direct the air AGAINST the direction of hair growth so it reaches the skin, and brush the opposite way as you go. Work section by section.

TEST WHETHER SHE IS ACTUALLY DRY. Part the coat with your fingers down to the skin and touch the skin itself in five places: base of the neck, under the elbows, chest between the front legs, base of the tail and trousers, behind the ears. Cool skin or damp roots means keep going.
On a golden this can take 30 to 60 minutes or more. It will take longer once the adult coat comes in.
not: Never leave her in a crate with a dryer pointed at it. Not at home, and tell any groomer the same. Dogs have died of heat stroke in cage dryers.
Do not trust the surface. A double coat feels dry on top long before the undercoat is.
Do not skip this because she is wriggling. A damp undercoat is how hot spots start.
entries.why: Moisture trapped under a dense coat causes acute moist dermatitis, which is what a hot spot is, and dense-undercoat breeds are over-represented. VCA describes them appearing so fast that an owner can leave in the morning and come back to a raw lesion the size of a pancake. A damp undercoat also compacts into mats, and mats then trap more moisture, which is a loop that feeds itself.
entries.vet: A hot spot is a red, wet, painful patch that appears fast and that she will not leave alone. Same-day call.

entries.title: Ear cleaning: more important for her than bathing
now: Every one to two weeks as maintenance. More often if she ever has allergies or a history of infection.
Clean AFTER a bath or a swim, not before, to clear the moisture that got in.
Method: fill the canal with a veterinary ear cleaner, massage the base of the ear, let her shake, then wipe the visible parts with cotton pads from the inside outward. No deeper than one knuckle.
Start now at 10 weeks with the same graded approach as the bath. Touch her ear, treat, two seconds. This is the highest-return grooming habit you can build in this dog.
not: No cotton swabs. They push debris deeper.
No alcohol, no hydrogen peroxide.
Do not squirt forcefully. Pressure can damage the eardrum.
Do not clean a painful, red or discharging ear. Call the vet first: if the eardrum is perforated, cleaner in the canal can cause deafness.
entries.why: She has drop ears, which means a poorly ventilated canal and a lifetime risk of otitis. Merck is explicit that preventing otitis externa means keeping the canals dry and well ventilated and keeping water out during bathing. For a golden this matters more than how often she is bathed.
entries.vet: Head shaking, head tilt, scratching at an ear, redness, odour, discharge, or pain when you touch the ear base. Any of those, call.

entries.title: Groomers and dog washes: not yet, and here is the date
now: Do the bath protocol at home for now. That gets you most of the socialisation value with none of the infection risk.

Book a meet and greet at your chosen salon: CARRY her in, feet off the floor, five minutes in reception, treats, no bath, out. The building, the smells and the dryer noise are what need socialising, not the tub. Ask first and go at a quiet time.

Book the real first appointment for about two weeks after her final DAPP dose, likely late October. Ask for a short introductory groom, 20 to 30 minutes: bath, quick dry, light brush, feet and face tidy.
Ask the salon directly: what vaccines do you require, do you separate puppies, how do you disinfect between dogs, do you use cage dryers. A good salon has ready answers.
not: No self-service dog wash until her series is done. Worse than a salon: nobody screens vaccination, the tub itself is the shared surface she would stand in, and she scavenges. You already have a bathtub, so there is nothing to trade against the risk.
Red flags in a groomer: will not answer questions, uses cage dryers unattended, suggests shaving a golden, or will not do a short introductory visit.
entries.why: Parvovirus is the concern, not germs generally. It is spread by swallowing virus shed in faeces, an apparently healthy dog can be shedding for two weeks before showing signs, and it survives in the environment for up to a year. Puppies from six weeks to six months are the most affected group. The counterweight is real too: her socialisation window closes around 16 weeks, which is the same date her vaccine series completes, and more dogs under three die from behaviour problems than from infectious disease. There is a genuine tension here and anyone who tells you otherwise is oversimplifying.
entries.vet: Worth raising honestly: she already walks on city sidewalks and scavenges, which is arguably a higher parvo exposure than a screened salon. If that risk has been accepted, refusing a salon purely on infection grounds is not consistent. That is a conversation for you and your vet.

entries.title: How often should she be bathed?
now: No schedule. Bathe her when she is visibly dirty, when she smells, or when she has rolled in something.
Realistically that will land somewhere between every 3 and 8 weeks for her.
Brush her weekly regardless. Brushing, not bathing, is what actually maintains a double coat.
If she rolls in something foul, bathe her immediately. There is no such thing as too soon when the alternative is leaving it in an undercoat.
Most apartment dirt is feet, belly, chest and rear. A damp cloth on those four places is the right tool, not a whole bath.
not: Do not run a calendar. The once a month rule has no evidence behind it. It is a number that circulates because it is easy to remember.
If you find yourself bathing her more than every three weeks with no reason, do not just carry on. That is a skin question for the vet, not a grooming habit.
Do not bathe a matted or tangled coat. Water tightens mats. Brush her out dry first, every time.
entries.why: Mainstream veterinary sources span weekly to every twelve weeks, a twelve-fold spread, which is itself the proof that nobody has measured this. The AKC says monthly for a golden; VCA says six to eight weeks; Virginia Tech says four to twelve; WSAVA says no more than monthly in a dry climate. Note the pattern though: dermatologists bathe dogs MORE often than groomers do, because in a dog with skin disease frequent bathing removes allergens and hydrates skin. The do not over-bathe instinct is a coat-cosmetics argument, not a skin-health one, and it applies to healthy dogs only. Over-bathing is real: surfactants strip the surface lipid film, and a dog has only three to five epidermal cell layers against a human ten to fifteen, so there is less barrier to spare. Signs you have overdone it are flaking, a dull or brittle coat, new itching that starts after baths, and pink skin at the belly and armpits. Under-bathing is the more likely failure in a city though, and for a golden it ends in matting and hot spots.
entries.vet: Odour that comes back within days of a bath is a sign to investigate skin and ears, not to bathe more often.

entries.title: How to bathe her, step by step
now: BEFORE she is in the room: door shut, room warmed to at least 72F. Run the shower hot for a minute to warm it.
NON-SLIP MAT IN THE TUB. Not optional. A dog whose feet slide has no control over her own body, and that is frightening. Many dogs who hate baths actually hate sliding.
Everything within reach before she is wet: shampoo with the cap already open, three or four towels, lickmat, treats, a jug or shower hose.
Brush her out dry first. Take her out to toilet. Cotton ball resting AT the entrance of each ear, not pushed in.
Water 98 to 102F. Test on the inside of your wrist. It should feel neutral, not warm. Two to three inches depth at most, or none with a running hose.
Start the water on her feet and rear, never her head.
Wet her from the neck backwards, thoroughly. A double coat repels water. If it is beading off she is not wet enough and the shampoo will sit on top.
Shampoo diluted, worked in with fingertips down to the skin: neck, back, sides, legs, belly, tail, rear last.
RINSE, THEN RINSE AGAIN. Plan on twice as long rinsing as shampooing.
Face last, with a plain damp cloth and no shampoo at all. Never rinse her head with a hose.
Squeegee the water out with your hands before the towel. It removes a surprising amount.
Cotton out, ears dried.
not: Do not bathe her in the kitchen sink. It works at 10 weeks and she will outgrow it within weeks, and you will have taught her a place that then gets taken away. Use the tub she will use for life.
Do not spray water into her ears. Wash the ear leather with a damp cloth.
No shampoo above her eyebrow line.
Do not take her outside for at least one to two hours afterwards, longer in winter.
Stop and dry immediately if she shivers, tucks up, or goes quiet and rigid.
entries.why: The rinse is the step people cut short and it matters more on a double coat than anywhere else. Shampoo left in a dense undercoat is a leading cause of itching and flaking after a bath. The test: run your hands through the coat feeling for slippery spots. Any slickness or foam means keep rinsing. Check the armpits, groin, under the tail, between the toes and behind the ears. Aim to have her wet for under ten minutes in the early baths.
entries.vet: If water gets deep into an ear: let her shake, that clears most of it. Wipe the visible part only, no deeper than one knuckle. Call the vet if in the following days you see head shaking, a head tilt, scratching at the ear, redness, odour, discharge, or pain when you touch the ear base.

entries.title: Paws after the sidewalk, and winter salt
now: A damp cloth or dog-safe wipe over all four feet after every walk. Twenty seconds.
Dry between the toes afterwards. She grows hair between the pads that holds moisture.

WINTER: rinse her feet in cool or lukewarm water, never hot, after every walk. Salt dissolves in water, so you do not need soap or a special product. Dip each foot in a shallow container, massage the pads, dry thoroughly.
Consider boots or a paw wax once the salt is down.
Full paw rinsing the rest of the year only when they are visibly caked.
not: Do not skip this because she was only out for five minutes. She scavenges off the ground, so whatever is on her feet ends up in her mouth.
Do not leave the feet damp. Wet paws left dirty are how yeast between the toes starts, which is the corn-chip smell and the constant licking.
entries.why: The ASPCA classes all ice-melting products as chemical irritants. Pellets wedge between the pads and burn, and then she licks them off. Serious poisoning is rare; the everyday problem is irritated cracked pads. Daily foot handling is also free training: it is what makes nail trims and the bath protocol easy later.
entries.vet: Constant licking at one foot, limping, redness between the toes, or a smell from the paws.

entries.title: Booties: mostly no, and the one time yes
now: Not for keeping her clean. A damp cloth at the door takes twenty seconds and costs her nothing.

Not at ten weeks. Boots change how the ground feels and plenty of puppies simply stop walking in them. Her live problem is getting her to toilet outside, so this is the wrong month to add a reason not to move.
WINTER SALT is the real case, and it is a New York case. Ice melt pellets wedge between her pads and burn, and then she licks them off. Buy them around November.
The other genuine cases: hot asphalt in summer, though walking at cooler hours is the better answer; an injured or post-surgical paw on vet instruction; broken glass, ice or rough ground.
Fit matters more than price. Measure her paw width on a hard floor WITH HER WEIGHT ON IT, because the pad spreads when she stands. Too loose and they fly off, too tight and they rub.
Take them off indoors. They are for the twenty minutes outside, not for the day.
not: Do not put all four on for the first time and go for a walk. That produces the high-stepping cartoon walk, and if that is her first experience she will fight them every winter after.
Do not leave them on a damp paw for hours. A closed warm boot on a wet foot is how yeast between the toes starts.
Do not use them to keep her pads soft and clean. Pads are supposed to toughen with use, and permanently covered feet stay soft, which makes every barefoot walk worse.
entries.why: Her pads are a sense organ. They are full of nerve endings and she uses them to feel the ground, judge grip and know where her feet are, and boots blunt all of that. Bare pads also grip better than most boot soles, especially on smooth or wet surfaces, so boots often make a dog less sure-footed rather than more. Dogs shed some heat through their paws too, which boots trap. Honest caveat: most of this is mechanism and veterinary consensus rather than controlled trials. Nobody has run the study. But the reasoning is consistent and the everyday cost of boots is real, so the bar for using them should be a specific hazard rather than tidiness.
entries.vet: Constant licking at one foot, limping, or redness between the toes is worth a look regardless of whether she wears boots.

entries.title: Teaching her to wear boots, before you need them
now: Do this in November, before the salt goes down, not on the first icy morning.
Step 1: boot on the floor. She sniffs it, she gets food. That is the whole session.
Step 2: touch the boot to one paw, food, take it away. Five reps.
Step 3: one boot ON for three seconds, food, off. Five reps.
Step 4: one boot on, walk two steps, food, off.
Step 5: two boots. Then four. Then four plus a short walk indoors.
Two to five minutes a session, twice a day. She should be eating throughout.
not: Do not go straight to four boots. That is the mistake, and it is the one that produces a dog who refuses boots for life.
Do not push on when she stops taking food. That means she is over threshold, and the answer is to drop back a step.
entries.why: Exactly the same protocol as the bath, and for the same reason: the first several experiences decide whether this is a normal thing that happens or a thing she fights. Boots are worth twenty minutes of preparation in November because the alternative is wrestling four boots onto a 50 lb dog on a freezing morning when the pavement is already salted.

entries.title: What to wash her with, and what must never touch her
now: A shampoo labelled for dogs AND for puppies. Soap-free, no fragrance, no dye, tearless if it goes near her face.
Dilute a squirt in a cup of warm water before it goes on her. Neat shampoo sits on top of a double coat; diluted spreads to the skin and rinses out far more easily.
Contact time for a plain puppy shampoo is one to two minutes. That is all it needs.
Conditioner: not needed on a healthy 10 week old puppy coat. It becomes useful around 6 months when the feathering comes in.
Oatmeal shampoo is a harmless default if her skin ever looks dry. It soothes and hydrates. It does nothing against yeast, bacteria or parasites.
not: NO FLEA SHAMPOO. She is 10 weeks old. Flea shampoos are EPA-registered pesticides and the common label restriction is do not treat puppies under 12 weeks. The label age is legally binding and it varies by product, so read the actual bottle every time, and if it does not state an age, do not use it. If she ever has fleas the answer is a vet-prescribed product for her age and weight, not a shampoo.

NO ESSENTIAL OILS, and check the label of anything marketed as natural. Toxic to dogs on the skin, not only swallowed: tea tree, pennyroyal, wintergreen, birch, pine, cinnamon, clove, peppermint, eucalyptus, undiluted citrus, ylang-ylang. Several are hepatotoxic and several can trigger seizures. If a dog shampoo lists an essential oil, put it back.
No dish soap. It is a degreaser designed to strip lipid films, which is the exact wrong action on a barrier three to five cells thick.

No human shampoo. Human scalp is acidic at 5.2 to 6.2; a dog coat is nearer neutral at 6.2 to 7.5. Honest caveat: WSAVA says whether that difference actually matters is not known. The stronger argument is that her skin is simply thinner than yours.
Baby shampoo is a one-time emergency substitute, not something to own. Veterinary sources contradict each other on whether even that is fine.
No vinegar rinses, no baking soda. Both are folklore. Baking soda is alkaline, the opposite direction from her skin, and leaves grit in an undercoat.
Medicated shampoos are vet-directed only. If one is ever prescribed, the contact time is the whole point: five to fifteen minutes on the skin, and rinsing early wastes it.
entries.why: Her skin is not a smaller version of yours. Fewer epidermal layers, a thinner stratum corneum and different follicle density all mean it is more sensitive to surfactants than human skin is.
entries.vet: Ask before using any medicated or insecticidal product on her, at any age.

entries.title: Never shave her, and what trimming is fine
now: Tell any groomer, explicitly and every single time, that she is not to be shaved.

What IS fine to trim: hair between the foot pads, monthly, for traction. The sanitary area around the vulva and under the tail once the feathering comes in around 4 to 6 months. Light tidying of ears, feet, neck and tail.
Brush weekly with a slicker brush and then a comb. Daily during a heavy shed. Brush the hair, not the skin.
not: DO NOT SHAVE HER, EVER, including in summer. The undercoat insulates against heat as well as cold. Shaving removes it, raises her heat stroke risk, exposes skin to sunburn, and can permanently wreck the coat: the undercoat regrows faster than the guard hairs and crowds them out, leaving her patchy and textureless.
entries.why: This is the AKC Chief Veterinary Officer position, not a grooming preference. People shave double-coated dogs in summer believing it helps them, and it does the opposite.

entries.title: Does she actually need a bath, or just a clean?
now: Three different things, and only one of them is a bath. Pick the smallest one that does the job.
WIPE, damp cloth, no water, 20 seconds: wet or muddy paws after rain, salt in winter, food and slobber round her mouth, dust, a bit of grass, tear crust at the eyes.

SPOT CLEAN, warm water and a cloth on one area, rinsed and dried: she stepped in poop, she sat in her own pee, her rear is dirty after a soft stool, mud up her legs and belly from wet grass, she vomited on herself, one sticky patch, she lay in something damp in the street.

FULL BATH, the whole dog with shampoo: she rolled in something foul, she got into the garbage, she is dirty all over rather than in one place, she genuinely smells, or diarrhoea has gone up her legs and tail as well as her rear.
For a poopy rear or a dirty sanitary area: warm water and a cloth, or hold just that end under the tap. She does not need to get in the tub for it.
If she stepped in poop, wash the foot properly rather than wiping it. She scavenges, so whatever is on that foot goes in her mouth.
Dry whatever you washed, properly, especially between the toes and anywhere the coat is dense.
not: Do not full-bath her for a dirty patch. That is the mistake that turns bathe when dirty into bathe twice a week, and the full bath is the only one of the three that costs her anything.
Do not use shampoo for a spot clean unless the thing is greasy. Warm water and a cloth handles almost all of it.
Do not leave her damp after a spot clean either. A wet patch under dense coat is how a hot spot starts, whether it came from a bath or a puddle.
Do not bathe her after surgery or with stitches in until the vet says the date.
entries.why: Rain and wet grass in a city produce a genuinely muddy dog several times a week, and if every one becomes a bath you strip her coat and undo the work of teaching her to accept the tub. Almost all real-world dirt on an apartment puppy is on the feet, legs, belly, rear and face, which are exactly the places a cloth reaches. A full bath is for whole-dog dirt.
entries.vet: Repeatedly dirty at the rear, or a soft stool leaving her messy day after day, is a stool question rather than a washing one. Bring it up.

entries.title: She peed after her bath
entries.lead: Most likely she simply needed to go. A bath means fifteen or twenty minutes held still, then more time being dried, and a 10 week old bladder does not hold much. A gap of twenty to thirty minutes afterwards is completely ordinary.
now: Straining, or posturing repeatedly and producing little or nothing
Blood in the urine, or urine that is pink, red or cloudy
Wet patches where she has been lying or sleeping, or constant dribbling. In a young female golden, call about this promptly.
today: Frequent small volumes rather than normal-sized pees
Excessive licking at the vulva, or a strong unusual urine smell
A sudden increase in drinking alongside more urinating
House training that was going fine and then clearly regresses
mention: That it happens after baths specifically, and whether it happens every time
normal: One ordinary-looking pee, normal squat, normal volume, twenty to thirty minutes after a bath, while she is loose and relaxed. That is the expected outcome, not a problem.
entries.say: If you call: say how often it happens, how much, what her posture was, and whether anyone was approaching her at the time.
entries.note: Telling the four causes apart. NEEDED TO GO: normal squat, full puddle, she was loose and relaxed, not being approached. DELAYED STRESS: normal volume, once, on the floor after a stressful event; arousal suppresses urinating during the event and the bladder empties when it drops. SUBMISSIVE: happens when a person approaches, reaches or looms; ears back, lips pulled back, avoiding eye contact, cowering or rolling over; usually a dribble not a full void. EXCITEMENT: no submissive body language, happens standing or walking during greeting or play. Never scold her for any of them. Reprimanding a submissive pee makes her more anxious at the next approach, and with a puppy already unsure about baths you would be attaching that anxiety to you. Clean it up in silence. Prevention: take her out immediately before every bath and again after drying, and the question disappears.

entries.title: Something is ON her coat and she is trying to lick it off
entries.lead: This is a poisoning question, not a grooming one. Whatever is on her coat, she will lick off, and a puppy will start within seconds. Stop her getting to it first, then work out what it is.
now: STOP HER LICKING. That comes before washing, before phoning, before anything.
Antifreeze, of any amount, at any time. Sweet-tasting and lethal. Emergency.
Petrol, motor oil, tar, paint, paint stripper, solvent, or any cleaning product
Rat bait or slug bait powder in her coat
A de-icer or salt product she is chewing at rather than just walking through
Anything you cannot identify that came off a street or a basement floor
Call ASPCA Animal Poison Control on (888) 426-4435 or Pet Poison Helpline on (855) 764-7661 BEFORE you start washing, and have the container if you have it. Some things are made worse by water.
today: Something sticky and non-toxic: tree sap, chewing gum, food. Not urgent, but do not cut it out with scissors, you will cut her skin. Work it out with oil or a proper detangler, then wash the area.
Skunk. Not dangerous, but do not use water first, it sets the smell. Look up the peroxide, baking soda and dish soap recipe before you start, and keep it out of her eyes.
mention: Where in the building or the street she found it, so it can be moved
entries.say: Say what it is if you know, how much, how long ago, whether she has licked any, and her weight and age. Ask whether to wash it off and with what, because for some substances water is the wrong first move.
entries.note: Grease and oil are the one case where dish soap on a dog is legitimate, because you need a degreaser. Use it on that patch only, rinse hard, and phone the vet afterwards anyway. For everything else, dish soap stays away from her.

entries.title: Her belly is swollen, hard or painful
entries.lead: Almost everything in this entry is an emergency. Normal is soft and painless. Hard or painful is never normal.
now: Swollen belly plus repeated retching that produces nothing. Do not wait.
A belly that is hard, tight or drum-like
Any swelling that has appeared or grown over hours
She cries, growls, snaps or tenses when her belly is touched or she is lifted
Restless, pacing, cannot lie down, drooling heavily, or front end down and rear end up
Belly swelling with pale gums, weakness or collapse
Any belly swelling when she may have swallowed something
today: A belly rounder than usual but soft, she is bright, eating, playing and not painful. Call today and take a photo from above and from the side. Puppies with worms get pot-bellied and she is only a week past Panacur.
Any belly change plus a change in stool
mention: Round only in the half hour after a full meal, flattening afterwards, in a thriving puppy
normal: A soft full rounded belly right after a big meal, comfortable to touch, settling within an hour.
entries.note: Classic bloat is a disease of large deep-chested middle-aged dogs, so a ten-week-old golden is not the typical case. That does not lower the urgency at all. In a puppy a distended painful belly more often means an obstruction, a heavy worm burden, or organ disease, and you cannot tell which at home.

entries.title: Coughing, or noisy or heavy breathing
entries.lead: Count her breaths first. Watch her chest for 15 seconds and multiply by four. Normal at rest is 12 to 30 a minute.
now: Gums, tongue or muzzle look blue, gray or purple
Breathing with her neck stretched out, elbows pushed away from her body, or her belly heaving
Rate well above 30 at rest, or you can hear real effort
Coughing up blood, or pink froth
She collapses or goes weak during or after coughing
She coughed suddenly while eating or after grabbing something and cannot settle. Assume it is in her airway.
today: Any new cough at all in an under-vaccinated puppy, even if she seems happy otherwise
Cough plus runny nose or eyes, sneezing, less appetite, low energy
Any cough lasting more than 24 hours
Coughing or noisy breathing that started after leash pressure on her neck and has continued since
mention: One or two isolated coughs after drinking fast or a burst of play, with nothing since
normal: Reverse sneezing is not coughing. She stands still, neck out, head back, and makes loud rapid snorting inhalations. It sounds alarming, lasts seconds to a couple of minutes, and she is completely normal afterwards.
entries.say: If it followed leash pressure, lead with that: I pulled hard on her collar and she sounded like she could not breathe, and since then I am hearing this. The vet needs the mechanism, not just the symptom.
entries.note: The classic honking cough is usually a small-breed problem and would be unusual in a golden. In her it is more likely infection or collar irritation. Those need a vet to tell apart and you should not try.

entries.title: Diarrhea, or blood in her stool
entries.lead: Two kinds of blood and they mean different things, but both mean call. Fresh red is bleeding low down. Black tarry sticky stool is partially digested blood from higher up, and people take it less seriously because it does not look like blood. Take it more seriously.
now: Bloody diarrhea of any kind, at any volume, at any hour
Black tarry stool
Diarrhea with a distinctly foul rotten smell
Three or more loose stools within 12 hours, or watery diarrhea
Diarrhea plus vomiting
Diarrhea plus lethargy, or refusing food, or pale gums
Diarrhea plus a painful or swollen belly
today: Any diarrhea at all, even one soft stool, in a bright puppy. She eats feces off sidewalks, which is a direct route to giardia and coccidia, and she has just finished Panacur.
Diarrhea lasting more than 12 hours
Mucus or jelly on otherwise formed stool
Visible worms
mention: One single soft stool followed by normal ones, no other signs
normal: A single softer-than-usual stool after a food change or a stressful day, with the next one normal and the puppy completely well. Photograph it. Anything beyond one stool is not this.
entries.note: The 48 to 72 hour watch-and-wait advice on most websites is written for adult dogs. Use hours for her.

entries.title: How to check her gums, and what the colours mean
entries.lead: Twenty seconds, and it is the single most useful check you can do when something feels wrong.
checks: Lift her upper lip and look at the gum above a canine tooth. Normal is pink and moist.
Press a fingertip firmly on the gum for one second, then lift. The spot goes white.
Count: one thousand and one, one thousand and two. Pink should return before you finish. Normal refill is under 2 seconds.
Note whether the gum feels wet or dry and tacky. Tacky is a dehydration sign.
If her gums are naturally black in patches, use a pink area, or check inside the lower eyelid.
now: White or very pale gums
Refill longer than 2 seconds, or the white spot barely refilling
Blue, purple or gray gums or tongue. That is oxygen failure.
Yellow gums, or yellow in the whites of her eyes
Brick red or muddy gums
Pale gums with weakness, fast breathing, cold paws or ears, shivering or collapse
Pale gums with bleeding anywhere, or pinpoint red spots or bruising
entries.note: There is no wait-and-see version of abnormal gum color. Pale means blood loss or shock, blue means oxygen, yellow means liver or red cell destruction. If you check and are genuinely unsure whether they look right, that uncertainty is itself the reason to call. On the way in, keep her warm, quiet and still.

entries.title: Very hard stool, dry pellets
entries.lead: Separate hard dry pellets that need visible effort and leave nothing behind when you pick them up are a score 1. That is a recognised dehydration sign, and it is also what a partial obstruction can look like.
now: Hard stool or no stool plus vomiting
Plus a swollen, hard or painful belly
Straining hard and producing nothing
Plus refusing food or lethargy
Blood on or around the stool
today: Two or more score 1 stools in a day. Call today.
No bowel movement at all in 24 hours. Most websites say 48 to 72 hours; that is an adult figure. A ten-week-old on several meals a day normally goes several times daily.
Repeated visible effort
Hard stool alongside drinking less than usual
mention: One firmer-than-usual stool followed by normal ones
Any stool change that lined up with the end of her Panacur course
normal: Firm, well formed, holds its shape, leaves a slight mark when picked up. That is a score 2 and it is what you want. Score 1 is not.
entries.note: Do not add oil, pumpkin, milk or a stool softener to get things moving. If an object is involved, softening the stool does not solve it and can delay the diagnosis.

entries.title: She seems flat, or is she just sleeping?
entries.lead: Total hours asleep is a bad test. Puppies sleep a great deal in short blocks. Use quality instead: four questions, when she is awake or when you wake her.
checks: Does she wake up normally? Say her name at normal volume. Normal: stirs, lifts her head, opens her eyes, orients to you. Abnormal: you have to touch or shake her, or her head lifts and drops.
Does she stand normally? Normal: stands, stretches, shakes off. Abnormal: will not stand, sways, staggers, knuckles a paw, or lies straight back down.
Does she still care about good things? Offer food, her favourite toy, the door. Abnormal: no reaction to food, or looks at it and turns away.
Is she bright between naps? Lethargy is dull while awake. Sleep is asleep a lot but sparkling when up.
now: You cannot rouse her, or rousing takes real effort, or she sinks straight back
Awake but will not or cannot stand, or is wobbly or falling over
Flat plus pale gums, refill over 2 seconds, or cold ears and paws
Flat plus any vomiting or diarrhea
Flat plus refusing food or water
Hiding, unusually still, reluctant to be touched, yelps or snaps when handled. That is pain, not tiredness.
Flat plus trembling plus cold
today: Noticeably duller than herself for more than 12 hours, even if she still gets up and eats
Sleeping through meals she would normally wake for
Play sessions much shorter than two days ago and not bouncing back
mention: A single unusually sleepy day after a big new experience, with normal energy next morning
normal: A lot of sleep in short blocks with bright alert windows in between, normal appetite, normal stools, normal play. Also crashing hard right after a walk or a training session. Overtired puppies get manic and bitey before they crash; that is normal too.

entries.title: She is limping
now: She will not put any weight on it at all, or will not stand
The limb hangs oddly, looks bent or rotated, or the paw drags
It started right after a fall, a jump off furniture, being stepped on, or a scuffle
She is crying, panting hard, trembling, or will not let you near it
Visible swelling, an open wound, or bleeding
More than one leg, or wobbly on all of them
A broken nail or a pad cut that keeps bleeding
Limping plus flat, off food, hot ears
today: Any limp still there after 12 hours, or that returns after rest
A limp with no obvious cause. Growing joints are a real concern in a large-breed puppy.
A limp that shifts between legs
She flinches when a particular leg or joint is handled
Licking obsessively at one paw
Something stuck in a paw. Sidewalks carry glass, salt and metal. Do not dig it out yourself.
mention: A brief limp lasting seconds after an awkward landing, gone within minutes, normal running since
normal: Puppies are clumsy, skid on smooth floors and hop briefly after a bad landing. Normal is seconds, then completely gone.
entries.note: Never give her a human painkiller. Ibuprofen, paracetamol, naproxen and aspirin are poisonous to dogs and can kill a puppy. Do not massage, stretch, bandage or splint it. Keep her quiet, carry her out to toilet, and call.

entries.title: She will not drink
entries.lead: Not drinking is more urgent than not eating, and much more urgent when anything is coming out the other end. A puppy has very little reserve.
now: Not drinking and vomiting or having diarrhea. This combination never gets a wait and see.
Not drinking for 6 hours or more with any other symptom
Gums dry, tacky or pale, or refill over 2 seconds
She drinks and immediately vomits it back
Weak, wobbly or hard to rouse
Skin over her shoulders, gently lifted, stays tented instead of snapping back
today: 12 hours with no water intake you have seen, in an otherwise bright puppy
Drinking much less than normal for a full day
Drinking much more than normal, or emptying the bowl repeatedly
mention: A day where she drank a bit less after a quiet cool day, then went back to normal
normal: Drinking less on a day she had wet food, more after play. Puppies drink in short scattered bursts; the daily total matters more than any one visit to the bowl.
entries.note: Do not syringe or force water into her.

entries.title: She will not eat
entries.lead: The advice that a dog can skip a day of food is written for adults and is wrong for her. Losing her appetite is the first sign of parvo, before any vomiting. In an incompletely vaccinated puppy, refusing food is a parvo screen, not a fussiness question.
now: Refusing food and wobbly, weak, trembling, cold, glassy, collapsed, or hard to wake
Refusing food and vomiting, or diarrhea, or a foul smell to her stool
Refusing food and pale gums, or refill over 2 seconds
Refusing food and refusing water
12 hours with nothing swallowed at all, whatever else she looks like
Refusing food when she may have swallowed something
today: Two meals in a row refused, even if she is bright and playing
Eating far less than usual for a whole day
Picking at food alongside hard pellet stools
mention: One skipped meal, next one eaten normally, bright and normal-stooled since
She has gone off one particular food but eats everything else keenly
normal: Eating less on a hot day or after a very big meal, provided she takes the next meal at full appetite and is otherwise entirely normal.
entries.note: Do not tempt her with human food, add things to the bowl, or hand-feed as a fix before speaking to a vet. If she will not eat, the vet needs to know exactly that, unaltered.

entries.title: Parvovirus: the one that matters most
entries.lead: Her DAPP series is incomplete. Protection comes at the final dose, sixteen to twenty weeks. She walks city sidewalks and eats things off them. Treat her as unprotected. This is why every threshold in this guide is shorter than what you will read online.
now: Any two of these together: flat when awake, refusing food, vomiting, diarrhea, refusing water
Bloody diarrhea, at any volume, at any hour
Diarrhea with a foul rotten smell
Diarrhea and vomiting together
Vomiting straight after drinking
Pale gums, refill over 2 seconds, cold ears and paws, collapse
today: One episode of anything above in a puppy who otherwise seems bright. One vomit. One soft stool. One skipped meal.
She has been somewhere with unknown or unvaccinated dogs and is even slightly off
mention: Where she has been walking and what she has picked up off the ground
entries.say: Say this word for word on the phone: she is ten weeks old and her DAPP series is incomplete, her last dose was 15 August. Then ask: could this be parvo, and where should I bring her in. They will often want her kept out of the waiting room. Carry her, do not let her walk or sniff on the way in.
entries.note: The sequence is lethargy first, then loss of appetite, then vomiting, then diarrhea. The early hours look like she is a bit quiet and did not finish breakfast. That is the moment to call, and the moment treatment works best.

entries.title: She ate something off the street, or something toxic
entries.lead: Call both the emergency vet and ASPCA Animal Poison Control. She eats things off sidewalks in a city with rodent bait, discarded medication and food waste.
now: Any suspected medication, human or animal, prescription or over the counter, including painkillers, antidepressants, ADHD medication, vitamins, cannabis
Rodent bait, slug bait, antifreeze, cleaning products, anything with a hazard label
Anything with xylitol: sugar-free gum, candy, some peanut butters
Chocolate, grapes, raisins, onions, garlic, macadamia nuts, alcohol
Drooling heavily, foaming, retching, staggering, trembling, twitching, seizing, unusually agitated or unusually flat after being outside
Sudden vomiting, diarrhea or bleeding with no other explanation
She chewed an electrical cord, even if she seems fine
A plant or mushroom you cannot identify. Photograph it, bring a piece in a sealed bag.
today: A small amount of something you believe is non-toxic and she is completely well. Call and describe it anyway.
She ate another dog's feces and is well. That is an infection exposure and the vet should know.
mention: The scavenging habit itself. What to do about a puppy who hoovers sidewalks is a real conversation, including leptospirosis, which is spread through rodent urine in puddles and is not part of her DAPP.
normal: Grass eating alone, in a puppy who is otherwise entirely well and passing normal stools, is common and usually not sinister. Unless it comes with vomiting.
entries.note: Have ready: what it was, how much, how long ago, her weight and age, and what she is doing right now. Never make her vomit, never give milk or salt, never give anything by mouth to soak it up.
entries.say: ASPCA Animal Poison Control (888) 426-4435, twenty-four hours, consultation fee around 95 dollars. Pet Poison Helpline (855) 764-7661. Call the poison line BEFORE you drive: they give you a case number and a treatment plan, so the ER can start work the moment you arrive instead of starting from zero.

entries.title: Seizure or collapse
entries.lead: Every seizure or collapse in a puppy this age is an emergency call. Some are a drive-immediately.
now: Any seizure at all. Phone the emergency vet the moment it stops. There is no wait and see for a first seizure.
A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes. Time it on your phone; in the moment they feel far longer than they are.
Two or more seizures in 24 hours, or back to back without full recovery between
Any collapse, even brief, even if she got up and seemed fine
Fainting during or after coughing, excitement or exercise
Collapse or seizure with pale or blue gums
She is unresponsive or you cannot wake her
Twitching, tremors, circling, pressing her head against a wall, sudden blindness
Off food and now weak, wobbly, trembling or collapsed
normal: Puppies twitch, paddle and squeak in their sleep and wake normally when you say their name. If she wakes normally and is instantly herself, that was dreaming.
checks: Do not put your hands or anything else in her mouth. Dogs do not swallow their tongues and you will be bitten.
Clear hard furniture and edges away. If she is on a sofa, get her safely to the floor.
Dim the lights, keep it quiet, do not crowd her.
Start a timer and note the time it began.
Film it if you can do so without getting in the way. A video is extremely useful to the vet.
Call while it is happening or the second it ends. Afterwards keep her warm and quiet and offer nothing to eat or drink until the vet says.

entries.title: She is straining and nothing is coming out
entries.lead: This is the one where the honest answer is that you cannot tell what it is and neither can a phone. Straining with nothing produced can be constipation, a blockage, or colon inflammation after diarrhea has emptied her out. They look identical from outside and have completely different urgency.
now: Straining and nothing produced, plus any vomiting
Straining plus a swollen, hard or painful belly, or she snaps or yelps when her belly is touched or she is picked up
Straining and crying out
Straining repeatedly for more than 4 hours with nothing produced
Straining plus refusing food, or lethargy
Producing only blood or bloody mucus
Any straining at all after a suspected swallowed object
If you cannot tell whether it is stool or urine she is trying to pass, treat it as urinary and go now
today: She strains, produces a hard pellet or two with obvious effort, and repeats it
Straining episodes across a day in a puppy who is otherwise bright
Scooting or licking at her rear repeatedly
mention: One brief harder-than-usual effort that produced a normal stool and has not repeated
normal: Puppies circle, sniff and adjust for up to a minute before going, and may make two or three attempts on a walk. That is positioning. The difference is effort and result: normal is fuss then produce, abnormal is push hard and nothing.
entries.note: No enema, no laxative, no oil, nothing by mouth. An enema is a veterinary procedure and giving one to a puppy with an undiagnosed blockage can do serious harm.

entries.title: She swallowed something
entries.lead: A blockage can compromise blood supply to the gut within hours, and a puppy with one can look completely normal for a day or two and then crash. A normal-looking puppy is not evidence that it passed. Only a vet and an x-ray can tell you that.
now: Vomiting, diarrhea, belly pain or tenderness, decreased appetite, straining or small amounts of stool, lethargy, or growling and biting when picked up or handled around the belly
Repeated vomiting, or vomiting that will not stop
Retching and bringing nothing up
The praying position: chest down on the floor, rump in the air. That is abdominal pain, not play.
Vomiting straight after drinking water
Swollen, hard or tense belly, or yelping when lifted
Something sharp, long and stringy, a battery, a magnet, or anything chemical
Choking, gagging, pawing at her mouth, heavy drooling, any trouble breathing
Something off the street when you do not know what it was. Call poison control as well.
today: A small smooth non-sharp object and she is currently completely well. Still call. The vet decides whether to x-ray and what to watch for.
Well but no stool passed since
You are not sure whether she swallowed it or dropped it somewhere
She keeps picking up and eating non-food things on walks
mention: She mouths non-food things but you have never seen her swallow one
entries.note: Never make her vomit, never feed her bread to cushion it, never give oil or a laxative, never pull on anything protruding from either end. Some things do more damage coming back up, and pulling on string can cut the intestine.
entries.say: ASPCA Animal Poison Control (888) 426-4435, twenty-four hours, consultation fee around 95 dollars. Pet Poison Helpline (855) 764-7661. Call the poison line BEFORE you drive: they give you a case number and a treatment plan, so the ER can start work the moment you arrive instead of starting from zero.

entries.title: She keeps squatting, or went again right after going outside
entries.lead: Frequent urination is expected at ten weeks. Frequent straining, and small volumes, are not.
now: She strains to urinate and produces nothing, or only drops
No urine passed at all in 8 hours
Blood in the urine, or urine that is pink, red or brown
She cries or yelps while urinating
Straining plus vomiting, plus a painful belly, plus lethargy
You cannot tell whether it is urine or stool she is straining for. Treat it as urinary and go.
today: She urinates outside and then squats again indoors within minutes, repeatedly. You cannot tell at home whether this is an infection, incomplete emptying, excitement, or incomplete housetraining, and those need a urine test to separate. Do not debug it yourself.
Many small squats producing a few drops each
A sudden break in housetraining in a puppy who had been getting reliable
Urine that smells strong or looks cloudy
Drinking and urinating much more than a few days ago
Licking at her rear far more than usual
mention: Normal-volume urination every one to two hours while awake with occasional accidents and no straining
Rolling over and dribbling when greeted or told off
normal: Frequent urination with good volume each time, no straining, no crying, clear pale yellow urine. That is a ten-week-old bladder, not a disease. Also excitement wees, and needing out within minutes of drinking or waking.
entries.note: If you can catch a urine sample naturally in a clean container, bring it. Never chase her with a dish.

entries.title: She is vomiting
entries.lead: Vomiting involves effort and belly contractions. Regurgitation is food simply falling out with no warning, usually right after eating. They are different and the vet needs to know which.
now: Two or more vomits within 12 hours, or three in 24 hours
She vomits, drinks, then vomits again. That cycle is a hallmark of both parvo and a blockage, and she has risk factors for both. Do not wait for a third round.
Blood in the vomit, or material like coffee grounds
Retching or heaving repeatedly and producing nothing
Vomiting plus a swollen, hard or painful belly
Vomiting plus pale gums
Anything in the vomit that is not food: fabric, plastic, stone, leaves
today: One vomit. Yes, one. She is bright, it happened once, nothing else is wrong, and you still call today. This is the threshold that is different for her than for an adult dog.
Repeated regurgitation after meals
Bile, yellow foam, more than once
mention: A single episode days ago with entirely normal appetite, stools, energy and gums since
entries.note: Do not withhold food or water, do not give a bland diet, do not give anything for nausea. Whether she eats next is a vet's call. The withhold-food-and-feed-chicken-and-rice advice is written for adult dogs.

entries.title: The training toys: which is for what, and which need you in the room
now: CLICKER. Use it today. Cheapest thing in the box and the only one that changes how fast she learns. It is the marker. See the marker word in Training.
FOOD PUZZLE. Use it today, on level 1, for one meal. It comes out of her measured food, not on top of it.
ONE DOOR BELL. Use the wireless button, mounted at her nose height by the potty door, on the lowest volume. Put the doorknob bells away as the spare.
PLAY GYM. Five minutes a day, supervised, standing on carpet, as a strange object to investigate and a tug station. Not as a jump. It has a few weeks of use left before she outgrows it.
SUCTION CUP TUG. Only with your hand on the rope and you sitting next to it. Never the self-play it is sold as.
TALKING BUTTONS. In the cupboard until about six months.
not: Nothing here stays on the floor when nobody is watching. Rope, squeakers, small parts and a wooden frame is the entire list of things the crate toys entry says must not be in front of her unsupervised. 'Indestructible' on a listing is marketing, not a test result.

Do not run three ways for her to say let me out. The doorknob bells, the wireless button and an OUTSIDE soundboard button all mean the same thing, and three signals for one need teach her none of them.
Do not add calories for any of this. Everything she earns comes out of the day's one container, so the bowl gets less. See the 10 percent rule.
Do not count any of it as exercise. Sniffing and problem-solving tire her out. Jumping and hard running damage her while her growth plates are open.
entries.why: Six of these seven are toys. One, the clicker, is a training tool, and it is the one that will actually make a difference. Enrichment matters, and it ranks below her sleep, her potty schedule and her recall. If a day only has room for one thing, it is not the play gym.
entries.vet: A missing piece off any toy, a swallowed rope strand, or retching with nothing coming up is a call, not a wait and see. See she swallowed something.

entries.title: Jumping on and off things: the sofa, the stairs, and her growth plates
now: Lift her on and off furniture, or put a step or a ramp there. Every time, including when it is inconvenient and she has already done it herself.
Keep the walk rule: about five minutes per month of age, twice a day. At ten weeks that is roughly twelve minutes at a time, and it is not a target to beat.
Grass, dirt and carpet before pavement, whenever you have the choice.
Stairs: carry her for now. A few slow steps up is far better than down, which is where the impact lands.
Put rugs or runners on the floor she does her zoomies on. Slipping is worse for her joints than the running is.
Tiring her out is a sniffing problem, not a running problem. A scatter feed and a food puzzle beat another walk, at every age and especially this one.
not: No repetitive jumping. No agility jumps, no jumping on and off the play gym, no ball thrown over and over so she sprints and turns hard on the spot.
No jogging with you and no running beside a bike. Not until she is grown, and for a dog her size that is later than most people assume.
Do not read her willingness as permission. She will happily do all of this and feel fine on the day.
entries.why: Her growth plates are open. They are soft cartilage at the ends of the long bones, and they are where a big puppy's bones are still lengthening. Repeated impact through an open plate can damage it, and the damage shows up as a joint problem years later rather than on the day it happens. In large breeds the plates are not closed until roughly 12 to 18 months, sometimes later. She is estimated at about 65 pounds grown, so she is at the wrong end of that range.
entries.vet: Limping, a yelp on a jump, a leg she will not put weight on, or stiffness after she has been lying down: see she is limping. Do not give it a week.
